note: CCAO-F review set of 193 questions (“Claude Certified Associate – Foundations · Ôn tập 193 câu”), supplied by the site owner on 2026-11-22; it replaces the earlier 60-question bank entirely. Question and option text, option order, answer keys and Vietnamese translations kept as published, apart from OCR repairs (dropped “ab” in “about”/“above”/“abbreviation”, stray bullet marks, a few typos) and numbered steps put on their own lines. The source has Vietnamese keyword cues and takeaways only; English explanations are translations of them. Domains were assigned by topic for this bank; weights are each domain's share of the bank, not an official exam weighting.

questions.question: A knowledge worker is explaining how to use feedback to improve Claude-supported work over time. Which description is most accurate?

options.text: Capture feedback as an aggregate quality score per run, since aggregate scores show whether quality is improving without requiring detail on individual issues.
Capture general impressions after each run and apply them as broad prompt rewrites, since broad rewrites cover more potential issues than targeted changes.
Capture feedback only after several runs so patterns emerge from the volume of observations, then apply changes based on the patterns rather than any single run.
Capture specific feedback after each run, translate it into targeted prompt or workflow changes, and observe whether subsequent runs improve.

questions.explanation: 'specific', 'targeted', 'observe' → a loop of specific feedback, targeted fixes and verification. Remember: Specific feedback + changes aimed at the right spot + measure again. An aggregate score or a general impression does not show what to fix.

questions.question: You are writing system-level instructions for a Project that supports recurring writing tasks. Which step should be performed first when writing the system-level instructions?

options.text: Refine the drafted instructions based on observed gaps from validation runs.
Validate the drafted instructions against representative requests for the Project.
Define the purpose of the Project and the boundaries the instructions must respect.
Distribute the finalized instructions to collaborators on the Project.

questions.explanation: 'first' → start with the purpose and the boundaries. Remember: Know the purpose and the limits first, then write, test, refine and share.

questions.question:
You are a knowledge worker deciding whether to escalate a Claude-generated output. Which is the correct order of decision steps?
1. Identify the audience and the impact of the output if it is wrong.
2. Document the decision and the rationale for traceability.
3. Compare the output’s risk profile to the organization’s escalation criteria.
4. Decide whether to use, iterate further, or escalate.
5. Assess the output’s accuracy, completeness, and any unverified claims.
questions.explanation: Context/impact → compare with criteria → assess the output → decide → document. Remember: 1, 3, 5, 4, 2. Documenting (2) always comes last; the decision (4) comes right before it.

questions.question: An analyst has been asked to compute summary statistics from an uploaded sales data file and produce a chart for a weekly report. Which output approach best fits the task?

options.text: Request a narrative description of the data in the chat response without computing values, leaving the summary statistics and the chart unproduced and the weekly report incomplete.
Use Code Execution to perform the calculations and generate the chart, then verify the computed results against the source data before sharing the output.
Produce a written placeholder for the chart in the chat response without generating the actual visualization, leaving the weekly report without the visual output it requires.
Ask Claude to estimate the summary statistics from a brief preview of the file, accepting unverified figures rather than running the calculations against the full uploaded dataset.

questions.explanation: 'compute', 'chart', uploaded file → Code Execution. Remember: Code Execution runs real code on the file → accurate, reproducible numbers; you still verify before using them.

questions.question: You are an operations assistant asking Claude to summarize 200 weekly metric records across multiple regions. Which output format communicates the data most clearly?

options.text: A series of regional narrative briefs, each describing weekly performance in paragraph form
A structured table with one record per row and one metric per column, sorted by region
A bulleted list of observations grouped by region without consistent metrics across entries
A narrative summary organized by region, describing trends and notable records in prose

questions.explanation: Many records, many metrics → a table. Remember: A table keeps a consistent structure and makes it easy to compare across regions and weeks.

questions.question: An operations assistant is using Claude to support process optimization for an existing intake workflow. The assistant has access to the current process documentation and recent cycle-time data. Which activity best uses Claude to support this process optimization task?

options.text: Use Claude to interview each team member who works on the intake process and synthesize the interview output into a redesigned workflow.
Apply Claude to predict the cycle-time impact of each proposed change and rank them so the team can implement improvements in priority order.
Generate an optimized version of the intake process based on industry benchmarks, then compare it to the current process to identify gaps.
Map the current intake process, identify likely bottlenecks based on the cycle-time data, and propose optimization options for human review.

questions.explanation: Use the data you already have + let humans decide. Remember: Claude analyses the real data and proposes; humans approve. The other options hand too much to Claude or ignore the actual data.

questions.question: A knowledge worker is explaining the purpose of an organizational AI governance framework to a colleague. Which description is most accurate?

options.text: A governance framework defines approved tools, allowed data, required reviews, and reporting paths so AI is used consistently and accountably.
A governance framework defines the training every employee must complete before using AI tools, with separate requirements for each tool the organization licenses.
A governance framework documents the AI policies the organization is legally required to adopt, focusing on regulatory compliance rather than day-to-day use.
A governance framework lists the AI tools the organization licenses and the cost of each, so users can pick the most cost-effective tool for each task.

questions.explanation: Governance = tools, data, reviews, reporting. Remember: It covers tools, data, reviews and reporting for everyday use; the other options cover only one part.

questions.question: You are organizing connected data sources for a team and must complete the planning steps before authorizing any connection. Which two planning steps must be completed BEFORE authorizing a new Connector? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Confirm the Connector is on the approved-vendor list maintained by IT.
Train every team member on the new Connector through formal training sessions.
Decommission any unused legacy Connectors that may still be authorized.
Migrate every existing report off the prior data source onto the new Connector.
Confirm the data classification of the source and the team’s permission to use it.

questions.explanation: 'BEFORE authorizing' → check approval and data classification. Remember: Approved vendor + data classification are the prerequisites. Training and migration come later.

questions.question: A knowledge worker often switches between Claude and another AI service while working on a long-running project. Which Claude feature most directly reduces repetitive context-setting between sessions?

options.text: Open every Claude session in Incognito mode, which prevents the conversation from contributing to Memory and therefore eliminates the cross-session continuity the project would benefit from.
Enable Memory and use the import capability to bring relevant context from the other AI service into Claude as a starting point for the project’s work.
Disable Memory entirely and re-paste the same context paragraphs at the start of every Claude session, even though Memory is designed to retain that context across conversations automatically.
Rely on a single static Artifact pasted into each chat as the only continuity mechanism, ignoring the Memory feature that is purpose-built for retaining work-relevant context across sessions.

questions.explanation: 'reduces repetitive context-setting between sessions' → Memory (+ import). Remember: Memory keeps context across sessions; import brings context over from another AI. Incognito does the opposite.

questions.question: You are a knowledge worker who decomposed a "draft a board memo" request into fifteen tiny steps and noticed the output now feels disjointed because related ideas were split apart. Which adjustment is most appropriate?

options.text: Combine the original request back into one unstructured sentence.
Remove all sequencing so the steps run in random order.
Subdivide each tiny step into ten more tiny steps for additional precision.
Consolidate related steps into fewer cohesive sections that group naturally connected ideas.

questions.explanation: Split too finely → the thread is lost → regroup sensibly. Remember: Decompose just enough: group related ideas into coherent sections; don't go back to one sentence, and don't split even further.

questions.question: You are configuring a new Claude Project for a specific recurring workload. Which Project configuration step should be performed first?

options.text: Add reference materials and instructions that the Project will rely on.
Test the configured Project on a representative request from the workload.
Invite collaborators to the Project and confirm the appropriate access levels.
Define the purpose of the Project and the recurring tasks it must support.

questions.explanation: 'first' → the purpose. Remember: The purpose determines the materials, instructions, access and how you test.

questions.question: You are an operations lead mapping production tasks to Claude model strengths to set realistic expectations. Which two production tasks fit Claude’s strengths most clearly? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Calculating the precise settlement value of a derivative contract using live market inputs
Synthesizing a single executive summary across many long source documents
Drafting a tone-and-audience-aware customer-facing email under human review
Issuing a binding legal determination based solely on Claude’s analysis of case documents
Monitoring a live sensor data stream and flagging anomalies as they occur in real time

questions.explanation: LLM strengths: synthesising text, drafting under review. Remember: Precise real-time calculation, binding rulings and real-time monitoring are not its strengths.

questions.question: An HR associate is preparing to use Claude on a sensitive personnel matter. The organization’s AI policy explicitly states that information related to ongoing investigations must not be entered into AI tools. Which response best aligns with the policy?

options.text: Enter the investigation-related information into Claude in an Incognito chat, since Incognito chats do not retain information and therefore fall outside the policy’s intent.
Enter a paraphrased version of the investigation-related information that removes identifying details, since paraphrasing addresses the spirit of the policy.
Refrain from entering investigation-related information into Claude and consult HR leadership for an approved alternative way to handle the matter.
Enter the investigation-related information into Claude only after the investigation closes, since the policy applies during the investigation period.

questions.explanation: An explicit policy ban → comply, don't work around it. Remember: Don't look for a way around it (Incognito, paraphrasing); ask for the approved channel.

questions.question: You are a product designer using Claude in a solution-design exercise. Which solution-design step should be performed first when using Claude?

options.text: Generate candidate solution concepts using Claude across diverse styles.
Produce detailed mock-ups of the chosen solution for stakeholder review.
Compare the candidate concepts against the constraints and select a finalist.
Articulate the problem the solution must address and the constraints in play.

questions.explanation: 'first' → define the problem + constraints. Remember: Know the problem and the constraints first, so you generate and compare solutions in the right direction.

questions.question: You are a marketing manager using Claude to ideate concepts for a campaign and must complete the framing steps before generating concepts. Which two framing steps must be completed BEFORE asking Claude to generate concepts? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Review the Claude-generated concepts and select the two strongest for further development.
Schedule the campaign launch and rollout dates with the agency.
Define the brand voice and the audience the concepts will address.
Select a finalist concept and prepare it for stakeholder approval.
Define the goal of the campaign and its success metrics.

questions.explanation: Framing = voice/audience + goal/metrics. Remember: These two steps set how to speak and what success looks like; the other steps happen after the concepts exist.

questions.question: You received a vague request to "look at our pricing." After discovery, the goal is confirmed: produce a structured competitor-pricing summary the team can act on, not new pricing ideas. Which strategy best fits the clarified task?

options.text: Use an open conversational strategy that explores competitor pricing iteratively across several prompts, allowing the structure to emerge from the conversation.
Use a comparative analysis strategy that contrasts the company’s pricing against a single named competitor, since pairwise comparison produces the clearest output.
Use a research strategy that gathers structured information about competitor pricing, names sources, and notes confidence in each finding.
Use a divergent brainstorming approach to generate a wide range of possible competitor-pricing observations, then narrow to the most likely ones.

questions.explanation: 'structured competitor-pricing summary' → structured research + sources. Remember: The task is research, not ideation; it needs structure, sources and confidence levels.

questions.question: You are an HR specialist reviewing data items proposed for inclusion in a Claude prompt. Which two data items are appropriate to include in a Claude prompt for a routine task? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: A redacted job description that the model will adapt for a posting.
A compensation-band summary that includes employee names and current salary figures for a specific team.
Accommodation request notes from an employee’s HR file needed to draft a role-adjustment memo.
An anonymized summary of an HR policy that the model will rephrase.
Employee identification numbers and hire dates for the team roster included to help Claude personalize onboarding communications.

questions.explanation: Include only masked/anonymised data, no sensitive PII. Remember: A and D contain no personal data; B, C and E are sensitive HR data.

questions.question: You are a project lead reviewing a teammate’s habit of using the same prompt template for every task regardless of type. Which feedback is most warranted?

options.text: The habit is ideal because a single template guarantees consistent quality across all task types.
Task type has no effect on the appropriate prompting strategy.
The prompting strategy should not change between tasks because adapting it wastes time and adds no value.
The prompting strategy should be adapted to each task type because one template does not produce equally strong outputs across all tasks.

questions.explanation: The prompt must fit the type of task. Remember: Research, calculation and creative writing each need a different prompting approach.

questions.question: You are a customer-success manager considering whether to escalate a Claude-generated response. Which factor most strongly raises the impact of the output and supports escalation before external use?

options.text: The response is an unchanged draft for a paying customer that includes a service-level commitment.
The response is a brief internal announcement about an upcoming team all-hands meeting.
The response is a casual rephrasing of an internal team status update.
The response is an internal draft summarizing the associate’s notes from a customer call for their own reference.

questions.explanation: External + paying customer + commitment → high impact. Remember: A commitment to a customer has contractual consequences; the other options are internal and low-risk.

questions.question: You are reviewing a Claude-generated report whose tone is confident throughout. Which question best separates plausibility from verification?

options.text: Can each specific claim be traced to a credible source or to the supplied input material?
Does the response open with a clear, well-framed statement of the main finding?
Does the response use varied sentence structure across sections?
Does the response cover the topic comprehensively based on its length and section count?

questions.explanation: Verification = trace each claim to its source. Remember: Confidence, length and style are only surface; verification means tracing every claim back to a source.

questions.question: A Claude associate is incorporating reviewer feedback that named two specific issues with a Claude-drafted brief. The rest of the brief was accepted as written. Which next step is most likely to produce a strong revision?

options.text: Rewrite the brief from scratch incorporating the two specific issues, since starting fresh integrates the feedback more cleanly than targeted edits.
Address the two specific issues and also revise unrelated sections to maintain a consistent voice across the brief after the edits.
Address the two specific issues and add a third improvement the associate identified, since combining reviewer feedback with self-identified improvements is more efficient.
Address the two specific issues directly, leave unrelated parts unchanged, and document the changes for the next review.

questions.explanation: Specific feedback → targeted fixes, without widening the scope. Remember: Fix exactly those spots, leave the approved parts alone, and record the changes so the review is easy.

questions.question: You are a communications manager validating a Claude-generated newsletter that includes a specific industry growth figure. The figure appears in three trade-press articles, but none of them link to the underlying study. Which validation step is correct?

options.text: Locate the original study referenced by the trade-press articles and verify the figure in the primary source.
Accept the figure because three trade-press articles repeat it.
Remove the source attribution and present the figure as common knowledge.
Use the highest figure across the three articles to make the newsletter more compelling.

questions.explanation: Several secondary sources repeating it ≠ verified → find the origin. Remember: Three articles may all copy one source; check the primary source.

questions.question:
You are a process consultant integrating Claude into an existing weekly workflow. Which is the correct order of integration steps?
1. Pilot the integrated workflow with a small group and gather feedback.
2. Document the current workflow steps, owners, and decision points.
3. Update the documented workflow and roll it out to the broader team.
4. Identify the steps where Claude can augment work and where humans must remain.
5. Define the inputs Claude needs, the outputs Claude returns, and the hand-offs around each step.
questions.explanation: Current state → where Claude fits → design inputs/outputs → pilot → rollout. Remember: 2, 4, 5, 1, 3: always capture the current state first, and pilot before a wide rollout.

questions.question: You are an operations assistant selecting a model for a recurring meeting-summary task that does not require deep reasoning and runs at moderate volume. Which selection best balances cost, speed, and quality?

options.text: Opus, which prioritizes depth at higher latency and rate-limit consumption.
Sonnet, which provides solid quality at moderate latency and rate-limit consumption for everyday work.
A custom model, which the Associate-level user would need to build and train independently.
Haiku, which is suitable only when the task requires the fastest possible turnaround.

questions.explanation: 'does not require deep reasoning', 'moderate volume', 'balance' → Sonnet. Remember: Sonnet is the balanced default; Opus is overkill; per the source key, Haiku is described as only for when maximum speed is needed.

questions.question: A business analyst has been asked to use Claude to extract requirements from a recorded stakeholder interview transcript. The transcript is approximately 90 minutes long and covers multiple topics. Which approach is most likely to produce a usable structured output?

options.text: Provide the transcript and ask Claude to produce a single ranked list of requirements, since a single list is easier for stakeholders to review than separate sections.
Provide the transcript along with a structured prompt that requests must-haves, nice-to-haves, open questions, and conflicts as separate sections.
Provide the transcript and ask Claude to summarize it; extract requirements from the summary in a second pass since two passes catch more detail.
Provide the transcript and ask Claude to produce a chronological list of every statement that contains a verb, then classify each statement as a requirement or not.

questions.explanation: 'usable structured output' → a prompt that specifies the output structure. Remember: Spelling out the sections required makes the output usable right away; summarising first can lose detail.

questions.question:
You are reviewing a Claude-generated competitor brief for unsupported claims. Which is the correct order of review steps?
1. Cross-check each specific claim against the supplied source material or trusted external references.
2. Decide whether to correct, re-prompt, or escalate based on the findings.
3. Document each unsupported or inconsistent claim with its location and severity.
4. Identify the specific factual claims, statistics, and citations in the brief.
5. Read the brief from beginning to end and flag any claims that feel surprising.
questions.explanation: Read → identify claims → cross-check → document → decide. Remember: 5, 4, 1, 3, 2.

questions.question: A senior manager is reviewing a colleague’s habit of never updating their team’s Project configurations because "if it works once, it works forever." Which feedback is most warranted?

options.text: Configurations should be updated on a fixed schedule regardless of whether the underlying policies and source documents have changed, since regular maintenance prevents drift.
Configurations should be left alone if the team is satisfied with current outputs, and any required updates should be handled at the chat level rather than the Project level.
Configurations should be updated only when output quality visibly degrades, since proactive updates risk introducing regressions in working configurations.
Configurations should be reviewed and updated periodically because policies, terminology, and source documents change over time, even when output quality has not visibly degraded.

questions.explanation: Configurations go stale over time → review them periodically. Remember: When documents and policies change, the output quietly drifts wrong; don't wait until quality drops visibly.

questions.question: An HR business partner is configuring two separate Projects for two distinct client engagements. Which configuration best prevents context bleed between the two engagements?

options.text: Set up each Project with its own distinct memory context, knowledge sources, and instructions, and verify that information from one Project does not appear in the other Project’s responses.
Skip Project configuration entirely and use general chats for both engagements, which provides no scoped memory contexts and offers no structural separation between the two clients’ work streams.

Configure both Projects to share the same memory context to reduce setup effort, even though shared memory between unrelated client engagements is precisely the configuration that produces context bleed.

Use a single shared Project for both client engagements with combined memory, knowledge sources, and instructions, on the assumption that Claude will keep the two clients’ contexts separate without configuration.

questions.explanation: 'prevents context bleed' → separation + verification. Remember: Separate Projects with their own memory, checked in practice; shared memory is exactly what causes context to bleed.

questions.question: You are an analyst reviewing a Claude response that addresses two of three required questions and skips the third. Which prompt element most likely needs strengthening?

options.text: The output format should be revised to allow Claude to determine the appropriate structure for each question’s answer.
The role assigned to Claude should be changed to a more specialized expert persona to increase response depth.
The context provided to Claude should be expanded with additional background detail about the subject matter.
The task statement should explicitly enumerate the three required questions and require an answer to each.

questions.explanation: One question skipped → the task statement didn't list it clearly. Remember: Listing every required question explicitly keeps any from being missed.

questions.question:
You are a Claude associate troubleshooting a recurring poor output. Which is the correct order of diagnostic steps?
(1) Form a hypothesis about which prompt element most likely caused the deficiency.
(2) Apply a single targeted change and observe the effect on the output.
(3) Read the output end to end and identify the specific deficiency.
(4) Compare the deficient output to the prompt to spot mismatches between input and output.
(5) Document the root cause and the resolution for future reference.
questions.explanation: Observe → compare → hypothesise → test one change → document. Remember: 3, 4, 1, 2, 5.

questions.question: A finance consultant is adapting a Claude-generated narrative for a quarterly investor update. Investors have a fixed time window for the call and expect the headline result and forward outlook to be clear early. Which adaptation is most appropriate for this audience?

options.text: Lead with the headline result, present the key drivers concisely, and close with the forward outlook.
Lead with a chronological recap of the quarter’s events, present the headline result at the natural end of the recap, and conclude with the forward outlook.
Lead with the forward outlook, since investors are most interested in what comes next, and present the headline result and drivers afterward.
Lead with the quarter’s operational highlights, present the financial result in the middle for context, and close with the forward outlook.

questions.explanation: 'headline result clear early' → result first. Remember: An audience with little time → put the result at the top (bottom line up front).

questions.question: You are a bank manager presented with a request to use Claude as the sole decision-maker on customer credit-line approvals. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Implement the design on a pilot basis and notify compliance only if issues arise during production use.
Expand the design so Claude both evaluates applications and issues final approval notices to customers directly.
Accept the sole-decision-maker design because Claude can process applications faster than a human review team.
Decline the sole-decision-maker design and propose Claude assisting analysts who retain decision authority.

questions.explanation: High-impact decision → humans keep the authority. Remember: Credit decisions have big consequences and are regulated; AI only supports.

questions.question: You are a research associate preparing inputs for a long task that references two lengthy regulatory documents, but only specific sections apply. Which approach best preserves context-window capacity?

options.text: Split each document into one-character pieces and provide them one at a time.
Extract only the relevant sections from each document and include those, omitting unrelated chapters.
Paste the full text of both documents without trimming to maximize the available material.
Skip the documents entirely and rely on Claude to invent the missing context.

questions.explanation: 'preserves context-window capacity' → include only the relevant parts. Remember: Trimming irrelevant content keeps the context lean and focused.

questions.question: A finance manager must select a Claude feature for a task that requires deterministic calculations across a multi-tab spreadsheet. Which selection best fits the requirement?

options.text: Use an Artifact alone for the calculations, which provides a stable editable surface for the result but does not perform the deterministic computation that Code Execution would run.
Use a standard chat prompt for the calculations, which generates text without running code and does not produce the reproducible computational output the multi-tab calculation task requires.
Use the Research feature for the calculations, which gathers and synthesizes external sources and is not the appropriate feature for deterministic computation on an uploaded spreadsheet.
Use Code Execution, which runs code in a sandbox to perform calculations on the uploaded file and produce outputs the associate can verify.

questions.explanation: 'deterministic calculations' + spreadsheet → Code Execution. Remember: Only running code gives accurate, reproducible calculation results.

questions.question:
You are a business analyst evaluating a Claude-generated business case against the agreed acceptance criteria. Which is the correct order of evaluation steps?
(1) Compare the business case with the source data and required topics.
(2) Document gaps and inaccuracies for follow-up or correction.
(3) Restate the acceptance criteria for the business case.
(4) Decide whether to use the business case, iterate, or escalate.
(5) Read the business case from beginning to end to form an initial impression.
questions.explanation: Criteria first → read → compare → document → decide. Remember: 3, 5, 1, 2, 4.

questions.question: A project lead is evaluating a Claude-generated status report against the project charter. The report will be delivered to a steering committee, which expects accurate status against committed milestones. Which set of criteria provides the strongest evaluation frame?

options.text: Speed of generation, visual presentation quality, and consistency with the formatting used in previous status reports.
Accuracy of facts against the charter, completeness against required reporting fields, and relevance to the audience receiving the report.
Length, formatting consistency, and tone appropriateness for a steering committee audience.
Readability, narrative flow, and whether the report tells a coherent story about the project’s progress.

questions.explanation: Accuracy + completeness + relevance. Remember: A steering committee needs it correct and complete; presentation is secondary.

questions.question: A support representative is configuring a Project for drafting customer-facing apology emails after service outages. The current custom instructions tell Claude to "be empathetic and casual, keep it short, and offer a goodwill credit." The customer-service team has flagged that recent drafts have been too brief, have offered goodwill credits in cases where policy does not allow them, and have used contractions that the brand voice guide prohibits. Which adjustment best aligns the configuration to the use case?

options.text: Keep the existing instructions and add a sentence telling Claude to consult the brand voice guide and the goodwill-credit policy that are attached to the Project knowledge base.

Specify the brand voice attributes (empathetic, formal, no contractions), set a minimum length, and instruct Claude to recommend a goodwill credit only when the attached eligibility policy permits one.

Move the brand voice guide and the goodwill-credit policy into the Project knowledge base and rely on the documents alone to govern tone, length, and credit decisions, without changing the custom instructions.
Replace "be empathetic and casual" with "match the brand voice guide," remove the instruction to offer goodwill credits, and let each draft determine its own length based on the incident.

questions.explanation: Three specific problems → fix all three in the instructions. Remember: B addresses all 3 problems directly and removes the contradiction ('casual'); the other options keep the contradiction or lack constraints.

questions.question: You are a knowledge worker summarizing common prompt failure patterns for the team. Which pattern most often produces vague or off-target output?

options.text: A prompt that names a topic but does not state the task, audience, or required output structure.
A prompt that explicitly names the role, task, audience, and required output format.
A prompt that includes a representative example of the desired output.
A prompt that adds clear constraints on length and tone.

questions.explanation: Missing task/audience/format → vague. Remember: Naming only a topic forces Claude to guess everything.

questions.question: You are refining a prompt over several iterations. The output drifts further from the requested template with each change. Which step is most appropriate?

options.text: Revert to the version of the prompt that produced the closest match and adjust from that baseline.
Stop iterating and accept the most off-target version.
Discard all prior versions and start with no record of what worked.
Continue making large simultaneous changes until the output happens to align.

questions.explanation: Drifting further each time → return to the best baseline. Remember: Keep the good version as a reference point and change in small steps.

questions.question: A Claude associate is identifying the bottleneck in a content workflow that takes too long to publish. The workflow has five steps: research, drafting, internal review, legal review, and publication. There is cycle-time data for each step from the past month. Which signal most directly identifies the bottleneck?

options.text: The step most recently added to the workflow, based on the assumption that process changes introduce the most friction.
The step where individual contributors report the highest workload in their weekly status updates.
The step with the longest queue or the largest backlog of items waiting to enter it.
The step with the highest average cycle time per item across the past month’s runs.

questions.explanation: There is cycle-time data → use it. Remember: Per the source key: the highest average cycle time is the direct signal. Assumptions or impressions are not data.

questions.question: You are a communications specialist preparing to describe Claude’s role in a workflow to multiple stakeholder groups and must complete the preparation steps before drafting messages. Which two preparation steps must be completed BEFORE drafting the stakeholder messages? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Archive the drafted messages in the corporate communications repository.
Define the key facts about Claude’s role and the boundaries that apply.
Schedule a follow-up forum to handle questions raised by the messages.
Send the drafted messages out and gather feedback for revision.
Identify the stakeholder groups and what each group needs to understand.

questions.explanation: 'BEFORE drafting' → content (facts) + audience. Remember: Know what to say and who you are saying it to before drafting.

questions.question: You are a marketing manager using Claude to research a new market segment. Which research step should be performed first?

options.text: Define the specific research questions that must be answered for the segment.
Validate the gathered information against authoritative external sources.
Submit a series of Claude prompts to gather information across the segment.
Generate a final research report combining every Claude output produced.

questions.explanation: 'first' → the research question. Remember: Without a clear question you don't know what to gather.

questions.question: You are reviewing items proposed for inclusion in a Project that supports policy summaries. Which two items are appropriate to include in the Project? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: The summary format and the audience expectations the summaries must meet
Active client case files maintained by a separate legal team for a different workstream
The current policy library that the summaries are drawn from
Presentation slides from a recent team training session on internal communication standards
Employee onboarding records used in a separate HR workflow managed by the same team

questions.explanation: Include only what directly serves the workload. Remember: Format/audience + policy sources; the other items are irrelevant or sensitive.

questions.question: You are sorting Claude output structural defects by which most undermines clarity. Which structural defect most severely undermines the clarity of the output?

options.text: Typographic inconsistencies appear throughout multiple sections of the document.
A single subheading is shorter than the other subheadings in the document.
The main conclusion contradicts the evidence presented in the body.
Two adjacent paragraphs present the same information using inconsistent terminology.

questions.explanation: Logical contradiction > formatting defects. Remember: A conclusion that contradicts the evidence breaks the whole message.

questions.question: You are a customer-success lead running an interactive workflow where each turn must respond quickly and the per-turn reasoning is light. Which selection best aligns with the requirements?

options.text: Choose Opus to maximize reasoning depth despite higher latency.
Choose any model because latency does not vary by model.
Choose Haiku to keep latency low and to handle a light reasoning load efficiently at scale.
Choose a model based on the alphabetical order of its name.

questions.explanation: 'quickly', 'light reasoning' → Haiku. Remember: Haiku is fast and cheap, suited to light, high-volume tasks.

questions.question: You are an operations lead and notice that a Project’s outputs have been drifting from the team’s current expectations. Which maintenance action should be tried first?

options.text: Review the Project’s instructions and reference materials against current standards.
Retire the Project and rebuild a new one from scratch with fresh content.
Switch the Project to a different Claude model in the hope it behaves better.
Continue using the Project and accept the drift as the new baseline of behavior.

questions.explanation: Gradual drift → check the configuration first. Remember: The cause is usually outdated instructions/documents; try the cheapest fix first.

questions.question: You are a project manager weighing workflow steps by how much leverage Claude integration provides. Which workflow step typically offers the greatest Claude leverage in a knowledge-work team?

options.text: Drafting and synthesizing across many sources for a downstream reviewer
Making final personnel decisions about hiring, promotion, or termination
Negotiating contractual terms with external parties on behalf of the company
Approving final deliverables for external publication without further review

questions.explanation: Strength: drafting + synthesis with review. Remember: The other options are decisions that need a human to be accountable.

questions.question: Before sharing a Claude-generated brief, an analyst is applying the AI Fluency Framework Discernment competency to evaluate it. Which review best reflects Discernment principles?

options.text: Conduct a systematic check of the brief against the task requirements, source material, and professional standards before sharing it.
Review the opening paragraph and the conclusion of the brief, since these sections typically reflect the quality of the full document.
Skip the source material check during review and rely on overall tone and logical flow as proxies for factual accuracy.
Accept the brief on the basis that it reads fluently and the subject matter aligns with the analyst’s professional knowledge of the topic.

questions.explanation: Discernment = evaluating output critically and systematically. Remember: Check against the requirements, sources and standards; fluency is not accuracy.

questions.question: An associate is responding to an executive who claims that Claude will eliminate the need for any human review on customer-facing content. The executive is the budget approver for the team’s AI tools. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Defer to the executive’s authority and remove the human review step from customer-facing content, monitoring the results closely for the first several weeks.
Acknowledge the productivity gains, then explain that human review remains essential on customer-facing content because of accuracy and brand risk, with specific examples.
Escalate the executive’s claim to a senior leader outside the team before responding directly, since the issue affects more than just the associate’s team.
Pilot the executive’s proposal on a low-risk subset of customer-facing content first, and use the pilot results to make the case for retaining human review on higher-risk content.

questions.explanation: Push back respectfully, with evidence. Remember: Acknowledge the benefits but keep the review principle for customer-facing content, with examples to illustrate.

questions.question: You are evaluating a Claude output that appears to contain hallucinated content. Which response step should be performed first when a hallucination is suspected?

options.text: Pinpoint the specific claim that appears to be unsupported by available evidence.
Notify the user community that the output contains a hallucinated claim.
Document the hallucination pattern in the team’s risk register for future reference.
Discard the entire output and regenerate the output with a fresh prompt.

questions.explanation: 'first' → pinpoint the specific claims. Remember: You have to know where it is wrong before you fix, report or document it.

questions.question: You are a content creator. A first response from Claude is accurate but uses inconsistent terminology that does not match your organization’s glossary. Which iterative change addresses the issue most directly?

options.text: Ask Claude to invent additional terms unrelated to the glossary.
Remove the topic from the prompt to avoid the terminology issue entirely.
Increase the requested length so the inconsistent terminology appears more often.
Provide the organization’s glossary and instruct Claude to use only those terms throughout the response.

questions.explanation: Missing glossary → provide the glossary. Remember: Supply the right reference material and clear constraints.

questions.question: You are a project manager reviewing Claude usage approaches that teammates have proposed for a project workflow. Which two workflow steps are well-suited for Claude support? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Synthesizing a literature review across many uploaded research documents
Deciding promotion outcomes for staff based solely on the model’s judgment
Issuing legally binding contractual commitments on behalf of the company
Drafting a structured project status update from a set of meeting notes
Approving a final external press release without any human review

questions.explanation: Synthesis/drafting = suitable; decisions/commitments = not. Remember: A and D are drafting and synthesis work; the rest need a human to be accountable.

questions.question: You are using Claude to redesign an employee onboarding workflow and must complete the high-level decomposition steps before specifying detailed artifacts. Which two decomposition steps must be completed BEFORE specifying exact email content and the schedule? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Negotiate the onboarding budget with the finance department.
Pilot the onboarding workflow with a small cohort of new hires.
Define the overall objective of the onboarding experience.
Roll out the onboarding workflow to every new hire across the company.
Identify the major phases of the onboarding experience.

questions.explanation: High-level decomposition = goals + phases. Remember: Know the goals and the phases first, then go into detail.

questions.question: A manager is deciding what changes to make while conducting a Memory maintenance review for a long-running workflow. Which two actions best support Memory quality over time? (Select two.)

options.text: Disable Memory entirely to eliminate the risk of stale entries surfacing in future workflow runs.
Delete all memories as the maintenance action to ensure a clean slate, then allow Claude to rebuild context organically through subsequent workflow runs.
Identify and edit or delete entries that are stale, inaccurate, or no longer relevant, and add context Claude has not automatically captured but the workflow continues to need.
Export the current memories as a backup before making changes, so prior context can be restored if a maintenance edit unintentionally removes information the workflow still depends on.
Leave all memories untouched on the basis that the workflow has been running consistently and no output-quality issues have been reported.

questions.explanation: Selective maintenance + a backup. Remember: Targeted clean-up with a backup first; turning everything off or deleting it all destroys the value.

questions.question: You are optimizing a recurring Claude workflow and must complete the diagnostic steps before changing the workflow. Which two diagnostic steps must be completed BEFORE changing the recurring workflow? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Identify the steps that contribute most to time, cost, or quality issues.
Measure the current workflow’s quality, time, and cost across recent runs.
Notify executive leadership of the projected savings from the optimization.
Document the revised workflow steps and update the team’s standard operating procedures.
Deploy the updated workflow across the team and monitor for adoption issues.

questions.explanation: Diagnosis = measure + identify the step causing the problem. Remember: Measure a baseline and find the problem step before changing anything.

questions.question: You are a project manager reviewing stakeholder messages that teammates have drafted about Claude’s role in a workflow. Which two messages are appropriate for stakeholder communication about Claude? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: An honest description of where Claude assists and where humans retain decisions
A clear statement of the limits and known failure modes of the integration
A claim that the model never makes errors and requires no quality review
A vague reassurance that "the AI is taking care of it" without further detail
A claim that Claude will handle every task without any human involvement

questions.explanation: Transparent, honest. Remember: State the role and the limits clearly; avoid over-promising.

questions.question: A learning specialist is configuring a Claude Project for a recurring course-design workflow. Which configuration approach best leverages a Skill alongside other Project elements?

options.text: Upload the supporting knowledge sources but disable the relevant Skill, eliminating the packaged capability the workflow needs and forcing each chat to reconstruct the procedure manually.

Configure the Project with custom instructions that contradict the Skill’s documented purpose, creating ambiguity about which guidance Claude should follow within the recurring course-design workflow.
Add the relevant Skill to the Project, upload the supporting knowledge sources, and write custom instructions that reference both the Skill and the knowledge.
Add the Skill to the Project but omit the supporting knowledge sources and any custom instructions, so the Project lacks the reference content and persistent guidance the workflow requires.

questions.explanation: Skill + knowledge + instructions working together. Remember: The three complement each other: a packaged procedure, reference content and standing guidance.

questions.question: The first output from Claude is partially useful but has tone and detail issues. Which two refinement actions are most likely to produce a meaningfully better output? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Increase the temperature setting and resubmit the unchanged prompt.
Add a specific tone descriptor and a concrete audience to the prompt.
Provide an example of an output that meets the desired standard.
Resubmit the same prompt several times and select the best response.
Append the phrase "please do better" to the end of the original prompt.

questions.explanation: Fix the prompt specifically: description + examples. Remember: Specific information and examples solve the actual problem; resending or 'do better' adds nothing new.

questions.question: A customer-success team member is reviewing a Claude-generated customer health-check report against the agreed deliverable list. The report covers all five required topics, but the renewal-risk section names only one risk factor where the deliverable specification calls for renewal risk to be assessed across pricing, product fit, and stakeholder change. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The report’s completeness cannot be assessed from the deliverable specification alone; the customer should review the output and confirm whether the renewal-risk depth is sufficient.
The report meets the topic-level requirements but the renewal-risk section is under-scoped against the specification and should be expanded before delivery.
The report does not meet the deliverable specification because a section that addresses only one of three required risk dimensions counts as a missing section.
The report meets the deliverable specification because all five required topics appear and the renewal-risk section is present in the output.

questions.explanation: All sections present ≠ enough depth. Remember: The accurate conclusion: it meets the topics but partly falls short on scope, and needs expanding.

questions.question: An operations assistant is redesigning a recurring data-processing workflow step to use Code Execution. Which two design choices best support reliable integration? (Select two.)

options.text: Define a brief output-verification step in which a human reviewer confirms the computed result against an expected range or sanity check before the output advances to downstream consumers.
Vary the input file format from run to run to accommodate the different source systems that supply the data each week.
Embed the Code Execution step inside the workflow without documenting the expected output format or the fields it produces.
Standardize the input file format the step expects, so each Code Execution run receives consistent input and produces comparable, verifiable output across recurring weekly cycles.
Eliminate the human review step that follows Code Execution, since the sandboxed environment already verifies that the code ran without errors.

questions.explanation: Standardised input + output checks. Remember: Running without errors ≠ correct results; you need consistent input and a sanity check.

questions.question:
You are a Claude associate running an ethics review on a Claude-assisted deliverable before publication. Which is the correct order of review steps?
(1) Confirm that transparency requirements are met for the audience receiving the deliverable.
(2) Document the review outcome and any changes made.
(3) Identify the audience and the potential impact of the deliverable on that audience.
(4) Make targeted revisions or escalate if a concern requires more authority to resolve.
(5) Examine the content for unsupported generalizations, fairness concerns, and accuracy issues.
questions.explanation: Audience/impact → check the content → transparency → revise/escalate → document. Remember: 3, 5, 1, 4, 2.

questions.question: A knowledge worker is explaining the cost, speed, and quality trade-offs across Claude models to a colleague. Which generalization correctly describes the trade-off?

options.text: More capable models generally consume less of the usage limit because their reasoning is more efficient, even though they run more slowly than lighter models.
Lighter models consume more resources per request than more capable models because they always require multiple passes to match higher-model quality.
Speed and resource consumption are independent of model capability; the difference between Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus is reasoning depth alone.
More capable models generally consume more resources and run more slowly, while lighter models are usually faster and less expensive.

questions.explanation: Stronger = slower, costlier; lighter = faster, cheaper. Remember: The basic trade-off between model tiers.

questions.question: You are an HR specialist reviewing model choices made by colleagues for various tasks. Which two model choices represent appropriate matches between the model and the task? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: A lighter, faster model for routine FAQ-style replies under tight latency budgets
A lighter, faster model for nuanced multi-document strategic synthesis
A higher-capability model for complex multi-step legal reasoning under review
A higher-capability model selected solely because it is the most expensive option
A higher-capability model for one-line keyword extraction at high request volume

questions.explanation: Match the complexity to the tier. Remember: Simple work that needs speed → a light model; complex work → a strong one.

questions.question: You are an HR specialist sorting potential ethical risks of a Claude-supported workflow. Which two risks pose the highest ethical concern in an HR-adjacent workflow? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Inconsistent use of the company’s preferred dash style across documents
Inconsistent tone and formatting across internal HR communications sent to employees
A clerical typo in a routine internal calendar invitation
Outputs that systematically disadvantage members of a protected group
Decisions that materially affect a person’s employment without human accountability

questions.explanation: Bias + lack of accountability. Remember: Discrimination and decisions nobody is accountable for are the real ethical risks.

questions.question: You are a knowledge worker reviewing a Claude-generated brief that asserts a "well-known industry standard" without naming any source. How should this assertion be handled?

options.text: Accept the assertion because the phrase "well-known" is reassuring.
Treat the assertion as unverified, and either source it from an authoritative reference or remove it.
Republish the brief unchanged because the claim sounds authoritative.
Strengthen the assertion by adding more confident wording.

questions.explanation: No source = unverified. Remember: Find a source or remove it; tone cannot replace evidence.

questions.question: You are a business analyst deciding which output-formatting and context-window practices to recommend to teammates. Which two practices represent effective use of the context window? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Paste full email threads related to the project into the context so the model has the complete conversational history.
Reuse the same context block across multiple requests to avoid rebuilding it each time.
Concatenate all source documents end-to-end with no separators between them.
Use clear section headers to separate different parts of the input material.
Trim irrelevant material before submitting the request to keep the context focused.

questions.explanation: Effective context = structured + lean. Remember: Separate the parts clearly and include only relevant content.

questions.question: Regenerating the same prompt gives you three noticeably different values for a key metric across three tries. You need a single reliable number for a finance summary due to leadership today. Given the inconsistency across regenerations, what is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Pick the value that appeared in two of the three tries
Treat the inconsistency as a warning; verify the source data
Use whichever value is closest to what you already expected
Average the three values and report the resulting mean figure

questions.explanation: Inconsistency = a sign it can't be trusted → go back to the source. Remember: A financial figure must come from the original data, not from a vote or an average.

questions.question: Claude turns a response into a separate Artifact rather than an inline chat reply mainly when the content is:

options.text: Generated during an active Research session
Written in a formal, professional tone
A response that simply runs past a few paragraphs of prose
Substantial, self-contained, and reusable

questions.explanation: Artifact = substantial, standalone, reusable content. Remember: The test is whether it stands alone and will be reused, not its length or tone.

questions.question: A Pro-plan user avoids Haiku 4.5 entirely, believing it is only a lesser model for people who cannot access better ones. Which statement corrects this?

options.text: Haiku 4.5 is the deliberate choice for quick, high-volume tasks
Haiku 4.5 is best reserved for tasks needing the deepest reasoning
Haiku 4.5 produces the highest-quality reasoning of the four
Haiku 4.5 is offered mainly to Free-plan users as an entry-level option

questions.explanation: Haiku = fast, high volume. Remember: Every tier has its place; Haiku is optimised for fast, high-volume tasks.

questions.question: A business user is unsure which model to pick for typical everyday writing and analysis. According to Anthropic’s guidance, which model is the recommended default?

options.text: Fable 5, the newest and most capable model
Haiku 4.5, the fastest and lightest model
Sonnet 5, the balanced default for most work
Opus 4.8, reserved for complex high-stakes reasoning

questions.explanation: 'everyday' → Sonnet. Remember: Sonnet is the balanced default. Model names as given in the exam.

questions.question: For external-facing or sensitive content, Anthropic recommends disclosing AI involvement in addition to which other safeguard?

options.text: Turning off the model-improvement training toggle
Attaching citations to the generated draft for source traceability
Qualified professional review before it reaches consumers
Switching to the account’s strongest available model

questions.explanation: Disclosure + qualified human review. Remember: Transparency + a person with the right expertise checks it before release.

questions.question: A team plans to run a Research session for every routine status question in a daily workflow. What is the key cost consideration they should weigh?

options.text: Research is unavailable on paid plans for daily use
Research lowers the account’s usage limit ceiling for the rest of the day
Research consumes usage quota faster than a normal message
Research runs on a separate budget that does not touch message limits

questions.explanation: Research = uses up your allowance. Remember: Research runs many steps and consumes quota; don't use it for simple questions.

questions.question: A strategist needs both careful reasoning and heavy multi-source gathering for a detailed market-entry analysis. Which combination does the guidance support for this task?

options.text: Concise Style, which balances depth and brevity for you
Research combined with Extended Thinking for reasoning plus source-gathering
Brainstorming alone, since ideation naturally includes reasoning and sources
Neither is needed, since a single Web Search covers everything

questions.explanation: Reasoning → Extended Thinking; multi-source → Research. Remember: Each feature meets one need; combine them for a complex task.

questions.question: A team is setting up a new recurring weekly task and has to decide how much reasoning depth it needs. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Write down what good output means, then run a real sample on the default tier, then compare that sample against the definition, then change tier only where it falls short.
Pick a tier by how important the task feels, then run it for a month, then write down what good output means, then compare the month’s results against that.
Run the task on several tiers at once, then write down what good output means, then compare the results against that definition, then keep the tier that did best.
Compare a sample of results with what colleagues produce by hand, then write down what good output means, then pick a tier on that basis, then run the task each week from then on.

questions.explanation: Define 'good' first → test → compare → adjust. Remember: Criteria first, evidence next, then targeted changes.

questions.question: One section of a long Markdown document in an Artifact needs a tone change for a different audience, while the rest is correct. What is the most appropriate way to revise it?

options.text: Highlight the section and request a targeted edit of that part
Retry the original prompt to generate an alternate full version
Start a new conversation and rebuild the whole document
Regenerate the entire document from scratch with a new prompt

questions.explanation: Fix it locally. Remember: Change only the part that needs changing and keep the parts that are right.

questions.question: A prompt that has produced excellent results all week returns one oddly disorganized answer. The user believes the prompt itself is fine. What is the best first move?

options.text: Use Retry to regenerate a fresh answer to the prompt
Rewrite the prompt from scratch to prevent future errors
Start a brand-new conversation and re-explain the whole task
Switch to a more capable model for this request

questions.explanation: A one-off glitch → Retry. Remember: Output varies; for a single failure, retry before editing the prompt.

questions.question: A new team member asks how the Claude model tiers actually differ from one another in everyday use. Which two statements are accurate? Select two.

options.text: The tiers differ only in writing style, so any of them may be used for any task at any time.
The deepest tier suits genuinely hard problems, and it consumes meaningfully more allowance.
Moving up one tier is the standard fix whenever a prompt comes back with a vague or shallow answer.
The lightest tier gives answers of the very same depth, only more slowly than the other two.
The mid tier is the fast, capable default, and it is the right pick for most everyday work.

questions.explanation: Opus = hard tasks, costlier; Sonnet = the default. Remember: A vague answer is usually down to the prompt, not the tier; lighter tiers are faster, not slower.

questions.question: You're briefing stakeholders on where Claude’s output needs extra scrutiny. Which single category should you tell them to always check against an authoritative primary source before use?

options.text: Brainstormed lists of rough, early-stage project ideas
Minor tone adjustments applied to a casual internal team message
Formatting and layout choices in a routine internal draft memo
Statistics, legal claims, citations, and direct quotes

questions.explanation: Verifiable facts with high stakes. Remember: Figures, legal points and citations are easily fabricated and costly if wrong.

questions.question: Within a single Project, which mechanism makes uploaded material available to every chat in that Project?

options.text: A Custom Style applied to the current conversation only
The Project knowledge base, shared across all chats
The conversation content of any one chat in the Project
The Project description field entered when creating the Project

questions.explanation: Project knowledge = shared. Remember: The knowledge base is where documents are shared with every chat in the Project.

questions.question: A support operations lead must classify a large daily backlog of short inbound messages, and separately needs one deep analysis of a tangled contract dispute. Which two choices fit? Select two.

options.text: Use the deepest-reasoning tier for the contract dispute, accepting the larger quota it uses.
Use the fastest, cheapest tier for the high-volume classification, where throughput matters.
Use the fastest, cheapest tier for both jobs, since the tiers differ mainly in reply speed.
Use whichever tier the team already has open, since the tier rarely changes what comes back.
Use the deepest-reasoning tier for both of the jobs, since the strongest option is never bad.

questions.explanation: Match a tier to each job. Remember: High volume and simple → light; complex and one-off → deep.

questions.question: You enabled a custom Skill and a colleague worries it will bloat every prompt the way project instructions do. Which fact reassures them?

options.text: A Skill can be created only by an org administrator
A Skill overrides profile instructions across the whole account
A Skill is injected into every prompt like instructions
A Skill loads only when Claude judges the task relevant

questions.explanation: Skill = progressive disclosure. Remember: A Skill loads only when relevant and does not occupy the context permanently.

questions.question: A strategy lead is planning a market-entry study and wants Claude to help with the research phase of it. Which two approaches are sound? Select two.

options.text: Accept the market figures Claude gives as final, since the answer reads confident and full.
Ask Claude to draft the research plan and its open questions, then have the team refine it.
Leave out the decision the study must support, so Claude is not steered toward an answer.
Use Research mode and check the citations it returns back against the original sources.
Ask for the finished conclusion in a single prompt and publish it with no intermediate step.

questions.explanation: Claude supports + humans verify. Remember: A plan that humans refine; Research with citations, and the sources checked again.

questions.question: With the Gmail connector active, a user asks Claude to prepare a reply to a vendor. Before actually creating that draft, the connector requires:

options.text: Nothing further, since the connector itself was already enabled
A one-time authorization that covers later email actions
The user’s explicit approval for that specific draft action
Admin sign-off before a reply draft can be generated

questions.explanation: Every action needs the user's approval. Remember: The connector asks for approval of each specific action.

questions.question: An analyst is presenting a Claude-assisted workflow to sceptical senior stakeholders next week. Which two things should the presentation include? Select two.

options.text: A claim that Claude will not make any factual errors once all its instructions are written well.
A promise that the workflow removes any need to check the output from this point onward.
Where a human still reviews the output, and why that review step has been kept in place.
A specific, measured example of what the workflow improved during the pilot it ran on.
A comparison of technical benchmark scores across each of the underlying model tiers.

questions.explanation: Persuasion = transparency + evidence. Remember: State clearly where humans stay in control and show measured results; avoid over-promising.

questions.question: A business user gets a vague, unhelpful first draft from Claude. According to Anthropic’s guidance, what does an effective prompt most reliably need?

options.text: The most capable model paired with a high effort setting
Forceful, capitalized wording that demands compliance
A single sweeping instruction covering the whole task
Explicit context, a specific task, and output format

questions.explanation: Context + task + format. Remember: The three core ingredients of a good prompt.

questions.question: Your conversation context has grown long, and the model is producing inconsistent outputs. Which context-management step should be performed first?

options.text: Start a fresh conversation and repaste only the essential prior context.
Switch to a different model in the hope that the new model handles long context better.
Summarize the prior conversation into a concise statement of the current state.
Continue the existing conversation and hope the model recovers consistency.

questions.explanation: 'first' → summarise the state. Remember: Per the source key: summarise first; once you have the summary, move to a new chat if needed.

questions.question: Which of the following features lets a user build an interactive working mockup that iterates in its own side panel?

options.text: Memory, which synthesizes background insights automatically
Web search, which returns quick factual lookups
Styles, which set tone and format per conversation
Artifacts, which hold reusable, iterable content separately

questions.explanation: Interactive mockup in its own panel → Artifact. Remember: An Artifact appears in a side panel and can be edited.

questions.question: You are setting up a Connector for a shared data source that several colleagues will use. Which Connector setup step should be performed first?

options.text: Document the Connector’s purpose and the appropriate use cases for the team.
Confirm the Connector is approved and the data classification is appropriate.
Connect the data source and confirm the authentication is working as expected.
Use the Connector in a representative task to evaluate its real-world utility.

questions.explanation: 'first' → approval + data classification. Remember: Don't connect anything before confirming it is allowed.

questions.question: Which SIAM process is responsible for restoring a service that has been degraded or interrupted?

options.text: Event management
Problem management
Incident management
Measuring and monitoring

questions.explanation: Restoring the service = incident. Remember: Incident: restore quickly; problem: find the root cause.

questions.question: A knowledge worker is preparing to use the Gmail connector with Claude for the first time. Which statement most accurately describes the connector’s behavior at the user level?

options.text: Claude searches and reads emails the user has access to in a read-only mode, and the user must compose any reply manually outside the connector.
Claude searches and reads emails the user has access to and sends replies on the user’s behalf for low-risk messages, with higher-risk messages routed to the user for approval.
Claude searches and reads emails the user has access to and drafts replies for the user to send manually, with each action requiring explicit user approval.
Claude searches and reads emails the user has access to and labels them according to user-defined rules, with reply drafting handled in a separate workflow.

questions.explanation: Reads + drafts + approval for every action; never sends on its own. Remember: The connector drafts, the user sends; every action needs approval.

questions.question: When refining a Claude output that does not meet expectations. Which iterative refinement step should be performed first?

options.text: Modify the prompt to address each identified weakness.
Identify the specific weaknesses in the current output.
Compare the new output against the original criteria.
Submit the revised prompt and capture the new output.

questions.explanation: 'first' → diagnose. Remember: You need to know what is wrong before you fix it.

questions.question: You are a Claude associate troubleshooting a Claude response that introduces facts not present in the supplied source. Which root cause is most directly indicated?

options.text: The prompt does not constrain Claude to use only facts present in the supplied source.
The prompt’s heading-based structure encourages Claude to generate placeholder content under each heading even when the source doesn't cover it.
The prompt asks for a comprehensive response, which leads Claude to fill perceived gaps with plausible-sounding but unverified detail.
The prompt asks Claude to act as a researcher rather than a writer.

questions.explanation: Missing grounding constraint. Remember: A constraint to 'use only the supplied sources' is the root fix.

questions.question: You are a platform architect designing an internal Claude-based assistant that serves both finance analysts and external auditors. Each population must access only documents permitted by their role. Where should role-based access control be enforced in the pipeline?

options.text: Inside the system prompt as a natural-language instruction that names the specific role-based access groups Claude should treat as unauthorized
At the retrieval layer, but relying on a single organization-wide access token shared across all roles rather than per-role scoping
At the retrieval layer, before any role-restricted content reaches the prompt construction step or the model
After the response is generated, by post-filtering content that should not have been retrieved

questions.explanation: RBAC at retrieval, by role. Remember: Data a user is not allowed to see never enters the context; a shared token breaks the permissions.

questions.question: You are selecting the documentation set that should accompany a Claude-based deployment at handoff. Which set is most complete?

options.text: Architecture overview, ADRs, component-level diagrams, runbooks for common operations, on-call playbook, and a list of known limitations
User-facing release notes, a marketing one-pager describing the deployment, and a customer FAQ
The original design proposal, its review comments, meeting notes from design sessions, and the approved requirements document
A project retrospective document, a lessons-learned summary, and a list of contributors

questions.explanation: Operational handoff = architecture + decisions + operations + limitations. Remember: Enough for a new team to understand it, run it and handle incidents.

questions.question: You are a solution architect designing a Claude-based assistant with access to 60 internal tools across multiple business domains. Loading every tool definition on every request increases token usage and time to first response. Which design pattern best addresses this issue without sacrificing capability breadth?

options.text: Group the 60 tools into five fixed categories and load one category per request based on a static mapping of task type to category.
Use a separate model call to condense all 60 tool definitions into a compact index that is prepended to each user turn for tool selection.
Apply progressive tool discovery so a curated initial subset is exposed and additional tools are loaded on demand based on the task.
Increase the maximum context length so all 60 tool definitions fit within a single request without exceeding the limit.

questions.explanation: Many tools → progressive discovery. Remember: Keeps full capability while cutting tokens; a static map is rigid, and a bigger context still costs.

questions.question: A knowledge worker has noticed that the same prompt for a recurring weekly task produces inconsistent outputs across runs. Some weeks the output uses the right sections but the wrong tone, other weeks the tone is right but a section is missing. The source inputs change each week but follow the same structure. Which cause is most worth investigating first?

options.text: The model is non-deterministic, so identical prompts naturally produce different outputs even when the prompt itself is well-written, and the team should accept the variation.
The source inputs vary too much from week to week, and the team should standardize the inputs before changing the prompt.
The team should split the prompt into separate prompts for tone and structure, since combining both in one prompt produces the mixed inconsistency the team is seeing.
The recurring prompt under specifies the audience, tone, format, and required sections, so each run drifts depending on what the model emphasizes that turn.

questions.explanation: Under-specification → drift. Remember: A prompt that states the required elements clearly reduces variation.

questions.question: A team runs two workloads that are alike in volume and subject matter. One is edited line by line by a specialist before use; the other is published automatically with no human reading it. Which consideration should weigh most heavily when choosing a tier for each?

options.text: The subject matter the two workloads share, since comparable material should be handled the same way for consistency of output.
The seniority of the people who own each workload, since the more senior owner is accountable for the more visible of the two.
How much a downstream human check would catch, since the unchecked workload has to carry its own quality with no safety net.
The volume of the two workloads, since equal volumes imply equal throughput needs and therefore the same balance of speed and cost.

questions.explanation: Whether there is a human safety net. Remember: A workload that is published automatically needs a higher-quality tier because nobody checks it.

questions.question: Preparing an AI-assisted work product for external delivery, a senior manager is applying the AI Fluency Framework Diligence competency. Which step best reflects Diligence principles?

options.text: Delegate accountability for the AI-assisted work product to Claude itself rather than retaining it as a human obligation, contrary to the Diligence principle that humans remain accountable for AI-assisted outputs.
Identify the elements of the work product that must be independently verified or corrected before delivery, and take ownership of those verifications as a professional accountability obligation.
