Skip verification of any element on the assumption that fluent output implies accuracy, even though Diligence requires the human to verify and correct AI-assisted outputs before they are acted upon.

Deliver the work product without independent verification on the basis that AI assistance shifts accountability away from the human, even though Diligence holds the human fully accountable for the output.

questions.explanation: Diligence = humans are accountable and verify. Remember: A human is always responsible for AI-assisted output.

questions.question:
You are a Claude associate assessing a proposed Claude use case before approving it for your team. Which is the correct order of assessment steps?
(1) Compare the use case against the organization’s policies and the relevant regulatory considerations.
(2) Document the assessment outcome and the rationale for traceability.
(3) Identify the audience, decision impact, and reversibility of the outputs.
(4) Decide whether the use case proceeds, requires modification, or is declined.
(5) Identify the data types involved and whether sensitive data is implicated.
questions.explanation: Impact → data → policy → decide → document. Remember: 3, 5, 1, 4, 2.

questions.question: An analyst is working in a long Claude conversation. The conversation contains roughly 60 turns covering an initial requirements analysis, several rounds of data review, and a current drafting phase. Recent responses have started to drift from the agreed requirements. Which step most directly addresses the drift while preserving the analyst’s progress?

options.text: Move the source data and the requirements into a Project knowledge base, then continue the drafting work in a new chat inside that Project.
Open a new chat and paste only the current draft, then continue refining it there without the prior requirements and data-review context.
Summarize the agreed requirements, the key data findings, and the current draft state, then continue in the same chat by reasserting the summary as the working context.
Switch the conversation to a model with a larger context window so the accumulated history no longer causes drift and continue without restructuring the inputs.

questions.explanation: Drift in a long conversation → summarise + restate. Remember: Per the source key: summarise and reaffirm in the same chat; opening a new chat with only the draft loses the requirements.

questions.question: You are reviewing claims about prompt iteration that colleagues have made in a recent training. Which two claims about prompt iteration are accurate? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Iteration is most productive when each change targets a specific diagnosed weakness.
Output comparison against original criteria validates whether iteration helped.
More iterations always produce a better output regardless of what was changed.
Iteration should stop only after every possible alternative phrasing has been tried.
Repeated resubmission of the same prompt is the most reliable way to improve output.

questions.explanation: Targeted iteration + measured against criteria. Remember: Changes aimed at the right spot, verified against the original criteria.

questions.question: A knowledge worker is defining what "workflow optimization" means at the Associate level for the team’s recurring AI-supported workflows. Which description is most accurate?

options.text: Replacing manual steps with Claude-supported steps wherever possible, since each replacement adds value by reducing the time the team spends on the workflow.
Reducing redundancy, removing low-value steps, and applying Claude where it adds measurable value, while keeping required reviews and quality gates.
Reducing the number of steps in the workflow to the smallest possible count, since fewer steps mean faster cycle time and lower error rates.
Standardizing every step of the workflow to a fixed template so each run produces identical output, without adjusting for variation in the workflow’s inputs.

questions.explanation: Optimisation ≠ maximum automation. Remember: Balance measurable value with quality control.

questions.question: A Claude associate is reviewing a Claude-drafted set of customer-segment descriptions for an internal marketing brief. One description applies a generalization about a demographic group’s purchasing behavior that does not hold for individual customers in the segment. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Add a disclaimer to the description, noting that the generalization may not apply to all individuals in the segment, and keep the underlying description unchanged.
Remove the entire customer-segment description from the brief, since any segmentation that involves demographic characteristics is likely to introduce similar issues.
Keep the description as written for the internal brief, since internal use does not carry the same risk as external publication of demographic generalizations.
Revise the description to focus on observed behaviors rather than generalizations about people, and validate the revision against actual customer data.

questions.explanation: Stereotyped generalisation → base it on behaviour + data. Remember: Fix the root of the problem and verify; a disclaimer does not fix bias.

questions.question: A Claude associate is evaluating whether to enable a Skill that was provided by an unfamiliar third party. Which two checks best support a sound trust decision? (Choose two.)

options.text: Treat the Skill’s appearance in a public listing as sufficient validation, without confirming the source, the requested permissions, or alignment with the organization’s approved-Skill list.

Enable the Skill immediately on the basis of strong external reviews, even though the source has not been validated against the organization’s approved-Skill list and the permissions remain unverified.
Verify the source of the Skill against the organization’s approved-Skill list before enabling it within claude.ai or any Project the team uses for its work.
Skip permission review on the assumption that the Skill cannot exceed the boundaries of the workflow, even though Skills can request access that the task does not require.
Review the permissions and capabilities the Skill requests and confirm that the requested access is appropriate for the task the Skill is intended to perform.

questions.explanation: Source + permissions. Remember: Check its origin and its access rights under least privilege.

questions.question:
You are running an optimization pass on a recurring workflow. Which is the correct order of optimization steps?
(1) Apply targeted optimization to the bottleneck step
(2) Roll out the optimized workflow to the broader team and document the change
(3) Identify the bottleneck step using measured time per step and queue length
(4) Map the current workflow steps, owners, and decision points
(5) Pilot the change with a small group and measure the effect against the prior baseline
questions.explanation: Map → find the bottleneck → optimise → pilot → roll out. Remember: 4, 3, 1, 5, 2.

questions.question: As part of a workflow redesign, a process analyst is applying the AI Fluency Framework Delegation competency. Which two criteria most directly inform Delegation decisions? (Choose two.)

options.text: The need for human creativity, empathy, or judgment in the step, which indicates whether the task is appropriate for AI delegation or requires the human capabilities Claude cannot provide.
The visual complexity of the workflow diagram, since steps with more connections and dependencies are more likely to require human oversight.
The seniority of the team member who currently performs the step, since more senior roles typically involve higher-stakes tasks that warrant human retention.
The reversibility of the task and the consequence of an error, which together indicate whether the step is safe to delegate to Claude or should be retained for human decision-making.
The length of time the workflow has existed in its current form, since well-established processes have been sufficiently validated for AI delegation.

questions.explanation: Delegation = nature of the work + risk. Remember: Does it need human judgement? Can a mistake be fixed? Those are the delegation criteria.

questions.question: You are a project manager at Orinexa, Inc. You are picking a Claude model for a new production workload and must complete the requirements steps before testing candidates. Which two steps must be completed BEFORE testing candidate models on a representative sample? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Choose a candidate model based on the requirements profile and known capabilities.
Sign off on the production rollout plan with the platform and security teams.
Promote the selected model to production traffic for the workload.
Define the quality bar, the latency tolerance, and the expected request volume.
Retest the selected model whenever a new model version is released.

questions.explanation: Requirements → candidates → test. Remember: You need criteria and a list of candidates before testing.

questions.question: A manager is about to tell her team that Claude will now produce the first draft of every incident report. What should the announcement make clear above all?

options.text: Which other departments have already adopted the same approach to their own reports.
How the manager tested the new arrangement before deciding to introduce it to the team.
What changes, what stays with each person, and where their review is still required.
How much time the change is expected to save the team over the course of a full year.

questions.explanation: Announcing a change = roles + responsibilities. Remember: Everyone needs to know what they are still responsible for.

questions.question: You are an operations lead evaluating prompting strategies that teammates have proposed for various task types. Which two strategies represent appropriate matches between strategy and task type? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Rigid templated prompting for early-stage creative naming and tagline ideation
Open exploratory prompting for early-stage strategic brainstorming on a new market
Rigid templated prompting for casual customer-feedback summarization with no schema
Open exploratory prompting for legal contract redlining against a clause library
Rigid templated prompting for monthly compliance reports against a fixed schema

questions.explanation: Creative → open-ended; fixed schema → template. Remember: Match the strategy to the nature of the task.

questions.question: A project manager is transforming a Claude-generated draft into a polished board memo. The board reads the memo before the meeting and expects it to be scannable, factually verified, and consistent with the organization’s standard terminology. Which set of refinements is most appropriate?

options.text: Tighten wording for executive scanability and verify each fact against source data; leave heading structure and terminology as written to preserve the draft’s voice.
Apply consistent headings, tighten wording for executive scanability, align terminology with the organization’s standards, and verify each fact against source data.
Apply consistent headings and align terminology with the organization’s standards; rely on Claude’s verification of facts, since the draft was generated from the source data.
Apply consistent headings, expand each section to give the board full context, and align terminology with the organization’s standards.

questions.explanation: Meets all 3 requirements: scannable + verified + terminology. Remember: Only B meets all three requirements.

questions.question: You are evaluating proposed workflow changes against whether they meaningfully improve the workflow. Which two proposed changes meaningfully improve a recurring Claude workflow? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Reorganizing the workflow document’s section headings to improve navigation
Updating the team’s shared workspace name to reflect the new workflow process
Adding a quality check on outputs before they enter the downstream process
Extracting the standard reference material into a Project to avoid repeating it
Labeling each workflow step with descriptive names to improve readability for new team members

questions.explanation: Real improvement = quality + efficiency. Remember: Changes to names or headings are cosmetic.

questions.question: You are reviewing colleagues’ responses to feedback received on Claude-drafted communications. Which two feedback responses are productive? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Deferring all feedback to a later revision cycle to avoid disrupting the current draft’s consistency
Declining to revise sections that were generated by Claude on the basis that the model’s output should be trusted as written
Incorporating all feedback received, including contradictory suggestions, into the next draft simultaneously
Mapping each piece of feedback to the specific change made in the next draft
Asking clarifying questions when feedback is ambiguous before acting on it

questions.explanation: Traceability + clarification. Remember: Record clearly what changed in response to feedback, and clarify what is ambiguous.

questions.question:
You are running a weekly feedback-and-adjustment cycle. Which is the correct order of cycle steps?
(1) Translate feedback into one or two targeted adjustments for the next cycle.
(2) Run the next cycle and compare results against the prior cycle.
(3) Capture the specific feedback received during the review.
(4) Document what changed, what effect it produced, and any remaining issues.
(5) Decide whether to continue iterating, switch approach, or escalate.
questions.explanation: Capture → adjust → run & compare → document → decide. Remember: 3, 1, 2, 4, 5.

questions.question: You have iterated a Claude prompt eight times, and the output quality has plateaued for the last four attempts. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: Iteration should stop and the current output should be accepted as-is regardless of remaining issues.
Iteration should continue indefinitely because more attempts always improve quality.
Iteration has reached diminishing returns and the next step is human review or a different approach.
Iteration should stop and the task should beandoned without communicating to stakeholders.

questions.explanation: Plateau → change approach/escalate. Remember: Recognise the limit of iterating and change direction.

questions.question: A finance manager is about to discuss a confidential pre-announcement figure with Claude. Which two settings best align with sound privacy practice for this conversation? (Choose two.)

options.text: Open the conversation in Incognito mode, which prevents the conversation from contributing to Memory and avoids persistent retention of the confidential pre-announcement figure across sessions.
Disable Memory contribution for the conversation if Incognito mode is not used, so the confidential figure is not retained as persistent context that could surface in later unrelated sessions.
Skip the privacy setting decision and proceed with default behavior, since the conversation will not explicitly instruct Claude to remember the figure.
Enable Memory contribution for the conversation so the context carries forward to support follow-up analysis in future sessions.
Treat the conversation as appropriate for default Memory settings, since the figure will only be discussed briefly and is unlikely to be retained.

questions.explanation: Confidential information → don't keep it long-term. Remember: Incognito or Memory turned off so the figure is not retained. (Data policy still applies.)

questions.question: You are a project manager working through a long planning conversation with Claude and must keep the conversation productive as it grows. Which two practices keep a long planning conversation productive? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Restate constraints and goals when the focus shifts to a new subtopic.
Open a new thread for every minor follow-up question to keep threads short.
Switch context aggressively between unrelated planning topics within one thread
Avoid summarizing so the model retains every original word it has produced.
Periodically summarize decisions made so far to compress the working state.

questions.explanation: Restate + summarise. Remember: Keep the focus and compress the context.

questions.question: You are an operations manager preparing a quick reference card for a team. Which description correctly characterizes the three Claude model tiers in general terms?

options.text: Haiku is fast and lightweight, Sonnet is the balanced default for most everyday work, and Opus is the most capable for complex reasoning at higher latency and cost.
Sonnet is the fastest of the three models because its architecture is optimized for speed rather than reasoning depth.
All three models offer the same reasoning depth and differ only in response speed and cost.
Haiku is the most capable model for the deepest reasoning, while Opus is the lightweight model for quick replies

questions.explanation: Haiku/Sonnet/Opus. Remember: The basic positioning of each tier.

questions.question: Before sharing a Claude-generated brief, an analyst is applying the AI Fluency Framework Discernment competency to evaluate it. Which review best reflects Discernment principles?

options.text: Skip the source material check during review and rely on overall tone and logical flow as proxies for factual accuracy.
Conduct a systematic check of the brief against the task requirements, source material, and professional standards before sharing it.
Review the opening paragraph and the conclusion of the brief, since these sections typically reflect the quality of the full document.
Accept the brief on the basis that it reads fluently and the subject matter aligns with the analyst’s professional knowledge of the topic.

questions.explanation: Same as question 48. Remember: Evaluate systematically, not on gut feeling.

questions.question: You are a knowledge worker preparing inputs for a Claude prompt. Which data type most clearly requires extra handling such as redaction or anonymization before being included in the prompt?

options.text: Job titles taken from the company’s public organizational chart
Generic product descriptions available on the company’s marketing site
Public press releases the company has already published
Customer government identifiers and full payment-card numbers tied to named individuals

questions.explanation: Sensitive PII + financial data. Remember: Public data needs no masking; identifiers and card numbers must be masked.

questions.question: A manager needs a comparison of six suppliers across five criteria. The information is currently spread across several separate Claude answers. What should she do first?

options.text: Choose the output format now, so that every further answer can be produced in that same shape.
Ask Claude to combine all of the earlier answers into one long document she can read through.
Agree which suppliers and which criteria belong in the comparison before asking for any output.
Ask Claude to rank the six suppliers straight away and work backwards from the ranking it gives.

questions.explanation: Scope first, format second. Remember: Pin down the right subjects and criteria first.

questions.question: A knowledge worker is briefing a stakeholder group on Claude’s limitations. The stakeholders will use Claude on customer-facing work where confident-sounding output that contains errors would cause real harm. Which limitation is most important to communicate clearly?

options.text: Claude’s knowledge has a training cutoff, so stakeholders must verify any time-sensitive claims against current sources before using them.
Claude can produce long, detailed responses that take time to read, so stakeholders should request shorter outputs when working under tight deadlines.
Claude’s responses vary across runs of the same prompt, so stakeholders should run each prompt several times and compare outputs before using any single response.
Claude can produce confident-sounding output that contains unsupported claims, so human review remains essential for high-impact work.

questions.explanation: 'confident-sounding output with errors' → hallucination + review. Remember: The question names exactly this risk; the answer matches it directly.

questions.question: An HR business partner is configuring a new Project for recurring policy questions from managers. The Project will be used across many chats by several HR team members. Which content belongs in the Project knowledge base?

options.text: The current employee handbook, the leveling guide, the policies-FAQ, and every email the HR team has sent about policy in the past year, for additional context
The current employee handbook only, with the leveling guide and the policies-FAQ attached at the start of each chat as needed for that chat’s topic
The current employee handbook plus prior versions of the handbook going back five years, so Claude can answer questions about how policies have changed
The current employee handbook, the leveling guide, and the policies-FAQ document referenced across the Project’s chats

questions.explanation: Current, shared, relevant documents. Remember: Nothing extra (emails, old versions add noise) and nothing missing.

questions.question: You are a knowledge manager structuring source material in the context window for a long Claude evaluation task. Which two practices produce a more effective use of the context window? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Repeat the same instruction at the start, middle, and end to reinforce it.
Place the most reference-critical material near the beginning or end of context.
Mark each source clearly with delimiters so the model can attribute claims correctly.
Mix sources together in a single block so the model can synthesize them freely.
Paste every available document into context regardless of relevance to the task.

questions.explanation: Placement + separating the sources. Remember: Information at the start/end gets more attention; delimiters help attribute sources correctly.

questions.question: A customer-success associate is drafting a prompt that asks Claude to summarize a customer issue from the case file. The case file includes the customer’s full government identifier, home address, name, account number, and the description of the issue. The summary the associate needs is about the issue. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Remove or redact the government identifier and the home address before submitting the prompt, since neither is necessary for a summary of the issue.
Submit the full case file and include an instruction telling Claude not to reference the government identifier or the home address in the summary.
Replace the government identifier with the customer’s name and the home address with the account number, since names and account numbers are less sensitive than identifiers and addresses.
Submit only the description of the issue and add the customer’s name for context, since the description plus a name is sufficient to produce a summary.

questions.explanation: Minimise the data before sending. Remember: Per the source key: A. An instruction in the prompt means the data has still been sent.

questions.question: You are an operations lead integrating Claude into a multi-person team workflow. Which integration step should be performed first?

options.text: Iterate the integrated workflow based on the findings from the pilot.
Pilot the integrated workflow with a small group on representative work.
Document the integrated workflow and onboard the rest of the team to it.
Identify where Claude adds value and where each handoff to a human occurs.

questions.explanation: 'first' → design the roles. Remember: Know what Claude does and what humans do before piloting.

questions.question: A Claude associate is evaluating a proposed use case in which Claude would issue final hiring decisions without any human review, applying the AI Fluency Framework Delegation competency. Which classification best reflects Delegation principles?

options.text: Appropriate for full AI delegation, on the basis that processing speed outweighs the human judgment, accountability, and consequence considerations that Delegation criteria require for final hiring decisions.

Inappropriate for full AI delegation, because hiring decisions involve human judgment, accountability, and consequences that Delegation criteria reserve for human ownership rather than autonomous AI execution,

Appropriate with light human review applied only to a sample of decisions, even though Delegation criteria reserve final hiring decisions for human ownership rather than sample-based oversight after the fact.

Inappropriate only because of system reliability concerns rather than accountability, even though Delegation criteria classify final hiring decisions as requiring human ownership regardless of system performance.

questions.explanation: Personnel decisions → humans. Remember: The right reason is accountability and consequences, not only technical reliability.

questions.question: An account manager has used Claude to extract requirements from stakeholder notes, Three requirements appear to conflict: two stakeholders specified mutually exclusive workflow steps, and a third requirement assumes an outcome the first two would prevent. Which step is most appropriate?

options.text: Select the requirement that has the strongest business justification in the source notes, set the conflicting requirements aside, and proceed with the selected one.
Flag the conflicts in the requirements document, document the source for each side, and route the conflicts back to the originating stakeholders for resolution.
Present all three conflicting requirements as alternative options in the requirements document, leaving the resolution to the project’s decision-making process later.
Apply Claude to propose a compromise wording for each conflict and submit the compromise to stakeholders as the proposed resolution.

questions.explanation: Conflicting requirements → stakeholders decide. Remember: The analyst doesn't arbitrate alone; trace the sources and hand it back to whoever has the authority.

questions.question: A project manager is defining how Claude can support requirements analysis for an upcoming engagement. Their team will conduct stakeholder interviews and review existing process documentation as part of discovery. Which activity fits this domain?

options.text: Use Claude to prioritize the requirements the team has already gathered, leaving the gathering itself to manual analyst work since prioritization is more time-consuming.
Use Claude to conduct the stakeholder interviews directly, with the analyst reviewing the recordings afterward to confirm the requirements Claude extracted.
Use Claude to synthesize stakeholder inputs and existing process documentation into a structured list of requirements with traceability to each source.
Use Claude to generate a complete requirements list from the project name and a short description, since requirements for similar engagements are largely standard.

questions.explanation: Synthesis + source traceability. Remember: Its strength is synthesis with traceability; it doesn't replace the interviewer or invent requirements.

questions.question: In a pilot of a new Claude-assisted briefing arrangement, three of eight testers report that the output is "not quite right" but say nothing more specific. What should the pilot’s owner do first?

options.text: Pause the pilot until the owner can sit with each tester and watch a full briefing being produced.
Ask the three testers for specific examples, with what the output said and what it should have said.
Rewrite the instructions to cover the areas the owner believes are most likely to be causing the trouble.
Ask the five satisfied testers what they did differently and circulate that as guidance to everyone.

questions.explanation: Vague feedback → ask for specific examples. Remember: Don't fix anything until you know the specific fault.

questions.question: A knowledge worker is iterating a prompt that has produced a partly acceptable response. Which refinement practice produces the strongest learning across iterations?

options.text: Change one identifiable element per iteration, capture the change and its effect, and adjust another element only after the first is settled.
Make several related changes in one iteration when they target the same weakness, and revert the whole set if the combined change makes the output worse.
Restart from a fresh prompt each iteration so that prior wording does not bias the next attempt, and pick the strongest response at the end.
Address every weakness the response showed in a single revision, then compare the revised output against the prior version.

questions.explanation: Change one variable at a time. Remember: You know exactly which change caused which effect.

questions.question: You are reviewing Connector setups that colleagues have proposed for various tasks. Which two Connector setups represent safe and appropriate uses? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Connector that links to the personnel-records system for team leads to support scheduling tasks
Connector that links to a personal cloud storage account where team members store working drafts alongside personal files
A8 a Connector that links to the team’s project management workspace under approved scope
Connector that links to the payroll system to allow team members to submit expense reports directly
A read-only Connector that links to the public knowledge base for reference content

questions.explanation: Approved scope, least privilege. Remember: Avoid HR data, salaries and personal accounts.

questions.question: You are handling a document containing mixed-sensitivity content before using it with Claude. Which data-handling step should be performed first?

options.text: Redact sensitive fields and replace them with appropriate placeholders.
Submit the redacted document to Claude for the intended task.
Classify the content of the document and identify which fields are sensitive.
Review the redacted document with a peer to confirm the redaction is complete.

questions.explanation: Classify first. Remember: If you don't know what is sensitive, you can't mask it.

questions.question: A communications manager is drafting a prompt for Claude to produce a quarterly newsletter for store managers in three regions. The agreed key messages, regional details, and a prior newsletter the team liked are all available. Which prompt approach is most likely to produce a usable first draft?

options.text: Provide the agreed key messages and the three regions, and ask Claude to choose an appropriate length and tone for store managers.
Attach the prior newsletter, and ask Claude to match its tone and structure while incorporating the new key messages for the three named regions.
Name the audience, the three regions, the length, the tone, and the agreed key messages, and reference the prior newsletter only as a tone example.
Attach the prior newsletter and the agreed key messages, and ask Claude to produce a similar newsletter for this quarter.

questions.explanation: A complete specification + an example with a clear scope. Remember: State every requirement explicitly; the example is only a reference for tone, so old content isn't copied.

questions.question: A senior project coordinator has been asked to use Claude to produce an end-of-year report covering finance, operations, and customer outcomes. The three areas have separate data owners and separate source documents. Which decomposition approach is most likely to produce a strong report?

options.text: Draft the three sections in parallel, each using a section-specific prompt, then concatenate and lightly edit the outputs into the final report.
Define the report goals, gather inputs per section, draft each section in its own prompt, then synthesize the executive summary from the drafted sections.
Prompt Claude once with all source documents and request the full report, including the executive summary, in a single pass.
Draft the executive summary first to anchor the report’s narrative, then draft each section so it supports the summary already written.

questions.explanation: Goal → sections → synthesis. Remember: The executive summary is written last, based on the real content.

questions.question: An HR team member is reviewing a Claude-drafted set of interview questions intended for use across all candidates for a single role. The questions will be asked in the same order to every candidate. Which review practice best supports fairness?

options.text: Review the questions to ensure they apply equally to all candidates, avoid assumptions about candidate backgrounds, and focus on the role’s actual requirements.
Review the questions and add follow-up questions tailored to each candidate’s resume so each interview can explore the candidate’s specific experience.
Review the questions for length and tone, since the questions Claude drafts are well-aligned to role requirements by default and need only stylistic adjustment.
Review the questions and rotate the order across candidates so no candidate is consistently asked the hardest questions first.

questions.explanation: Fairness = the same for everyone + no bias + job-related. Remember: Standardised, job-related questions reduce bias.

questions.question: You are an analyst fact-checking a Claude-generated report. Two cited sources give conflicting dates for the same event. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Choose the more recent date on the basis that later sources typically reflect updated or corrected information.
Locate a primary or authoritative source for the event and use the date that source confirms.
Average the two conflicting dates and use the average.
Publish both dates without resolving the conflict and let the reader choose.

questions.explanation: Conflicting facts → the primary source. Remember: Resolve it with the authoritative original source.

questions.question: A Claude associate is troubleshooting a Claude response that addressed only one of three required questions in a prompt. The prompt listed all three questions in a single paragraph separated by commas. Which root cause is most likely?

options.text: The prompt’s task statement did not enumerate the three required questions explicitly enough for Claude to address each one in turn.
The prompt’s required questions were addressed implicitly across the response, even though the response did not visibly answer each question.
The prompt was too long and Claude focused on the question with the strongest grounding in the surrounding context.
The prompt’s audience and tone specification overshadowed the task statement, so Claude prioritized voice over coverage.

questions.explanation: Not listed explicitly. Remember: Number or separate each question.

questions.question: You are evaluating whether a "redesign new-hire onboarding” request should be decomposed before prompting Claude. Which feature of the request most strongly indicates decomposition will help?

options.text: The request requires multiple distinct outputs: a process map, supporting materials, and a measurement plan.
The request involves content the associate has produced many times before and knows can be handled in a single well-structured prompt.
The request is for a single structured document that can be produced from one set of inputs in one prompt.
The request involves a single well-defined output with a clear input and a familiar format.

questions.explanation: Several different deliverables → decompose. Remember: The other options all describe cases where one prompt is enough.

questions.question:
You are decomposing a “build a customer journey map” request. Which is the correct order of decomposed steps?
(1) Identify the touchpoints the customer encounters during each stage.
(2) Define the persona and the journey scope to be mapped.
(3) Capture pain points and opportunities at each touchpoint.
(4) Synthesize the findings into the final journey-map artifact.
(5) Identify the major stages the persona moves through.
questions.explanation: Persona → stages → touchpoints → pain points → synthesis. Remember: Per the source key: 2, 5, 1, 3, 4.

questions.question: A sales manager is iterating on a Claude-generated solution prototype after a stakeholder review identified two specific concerns. The rest of the prototype was accepted as written. Which iteration approach is most likely to produce a strong next version?

options.text: Rewrite the prototype from scratch incorporating the two specific concerns, since starting fresh integrates the feedback more cleanly than targeted edits.
Address the two specific concerns and also revise unrelated sections to maintain consistent voice across the prototype after the edits.
Address the two specific concerns and add a third improvement the associate identified, since combining stakeholder feedback with self-identified improvements is more efficient.
Address the two specific concerns directly, leave unrelated parts unchanged, and document the changes for the next review.

questions.explanation: Same as question 21. Remember: Targeted fixes, without widening the scope.

questions.question: A communications officer must publish a Claude-drafted market briefing on the company blog within the hour. Claude used web search to produce it, and every figure in the draft carries a citation. What is the appropriate first step before she publishes?

options.text: Open the cited sources and confirm that each figure in the draft does appear in the page it points to.
Add a line at the foot of the briefing noting that it was prepared with the help of an AI assistant.
Regenerate the briefing in a fresh conversation, and publish if the two drafts report the same figures.
Ask Claude how confident it is in each figure, and revise the ones it rates as least confident.

questions.explanation: Has a citation ≠ correct → open the source and check. Remember: Citations can be wrong or not match; confirm them directly.

questions.question: After importing context from another AI platform into Claude’s Memory, a knowledge worker notices that some imported details did not appear in subsequent responses. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.text: Imported memories are stored separately from regular memories and cannot be referenced in any chat, so missing details reflect an architectural separation rather than imperfect import incorporation.
Memory imports are experimental, and Claude might not successfully incorporate all imported content; missing details can be added manually through Settings > Capabilities as a fallback.
The import transfers every detail as a rule, and any missing content reflects a deliberate choice by Claude to omit the information rather than the documented experimental nature of imports.
Memory imports overwrite all prior memories on completion, so any details that appear missing must have been deleted by the import process rather than not incorporated during the import itself.

questions.explanation: Import = experimental. Remember: Per the documentation: import is experimental, and details can be added manually.

questions.question: A Claude associate is applying the AI Fluency Framework Diligence competency to ongoing Claude usage. Which practice best reflects Diligence in a governance context?

options.text: Apply organizational AI policies only in high-visibility situations where usage is likely to be observed or reviewed by others.
Apply organizational AI policies during onboarding as a foundational training step, document that each associate has reviewed them, and treat that record as evidence of ongoing compliance.
Defer all policy application to a centralized compliance team, treating individual usage as outside personal responsibility.
Apply organizational AI policies consistently as a sustained professional habit, identify gaps between actual usage and the policies, and take corrective action to close those gaps over time.

questions.explanation: Diligence = continuous, proactive, personally accountable. Remember: Compliance is a regular habit, not a one-off.

questions.question: You are a procurement associate decomposing a vendor-evaluation task. Which dependency ordering reflects sound sequencing?

options.text: Skip criteria and ask Claude to produce a vendor recommendation from no inputs.
Rank vendors before any data is collected.
Score vendors first and decide on the criteria afterward.
Define evaluation criteria first, gather vendor data against those criteria, then score and rank.

questions.explanation: Criteria → data → scoring → ranking. Remember: The natural dependency order.

questions.question:
You are a senior analyst using Claude to analyze requirements from several stakeholder sources. Which is the correct order of steps?
(1) Group related requirements and flag conflicts or ambiguities for stakeholder review,
(2) Validate the structured output against the original sources for accuracy and completeness.
(3) Submit the consolidated inputs to Claude with a structured extraction prompt.
(4) Gather and label the source materials so each requirement can be traced.
(5) Document the final requirements set with source traceability and status.
questions.explanation: Gather & label → (per the key) group → extract → validate → document. Remember: Per the source key: 4, 1, 3, 2, 5.

questions.question: A knowledge worker is applying the AI Fluency Framework Description competency while revising an underperforming prompt. Which revision best reflects Description principles?

options.text: Specify the task scope, the required output format, the audience, and the relevant constraints with sufficient clarity that the prompt produces a useful, reliable output on the next run.

Add length to the prompt by inserting filler text that does not specify task scope, output format, audience, or constraints, leaving the original specification gaps in the underperforming prompt unaddressed.

Remove the existing context from the prompt and submit only the bare task statement, eliminating the audience, format, and constraint information that Description principles call for in a clear specification.
Replace the specific instructions with generic phrasing that broadens the task scope, undoing the specification work that Description principles require for a reliable, useful output on the next run.

questions.explanation: Description = a clear specification. Remember: Scope + format + audience + constraints.

questions.question:
You are a knowledge worker transitioning from a long, drifting conversation into a fresh focused session. Which is the correct order of transition steps?
(1) Begin a new chat and paste the summary as its starting context.
(2) Summarize the goals, key decisions, and open questions from the long conversation.
(3) Identify which references should persist beyond the current chat.
(4) Move persistent references into a Project’s knowledge base or attach them as needed.
(5) Confirm the new chat is on-task before continuing the work.
questions.explanation: Summarise → pick the documents → save → new chat → confirm. Remember: 2, 3, 4, 1, 5.

questions.question: You are validating evaluation criteria proposed for a Claude-generated business brief. Which three criteria are valid for evaluating a Claude-generated brief? (Choose three.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Alignment of the output with the requested format and length constraints
Consistency of the writing style with the organization’s established tone guidelines
Presence of an executive summary section as a structural completeness check
Factual accuracy of the claims made against the supplied source material
Total word count of the output relative to industry benchmarks for business briefs

questions.explanation: Format + tone + accuracy. Remember: Per the source key: A, B, D. Word count compared with the industry is not a quality criterion.

questions.question: You are an operations team member preparing inputs to summarize customer feedback. The feedback file mixes public quotations with personal contact details. Which preparation approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Replace the feedback content with the personal contact details and ask Claude to invent the missing feedback.
Extract only the feedback content needed for the summary, redact or anonymize personal contact details, and submit the trimmed input.
Submit the entire file unchanged so Claude has complete context.
Strip out the feedback content and submit only the personal contact details.

questions.explanation: Minimise + mask PII. Remember: Send only what is needed.

questions.question: Production monitoring shows that follow-up queries like “summarize what we learned about market trends" consistently take 40+ seconds. Investigation reveals the coordinator spawns the synthesis subagent for each summarization request, passing 80K+ tokens of accumulated findings. The coordinator already has these findings in its context from orchestrating the research. What’s the most effective way to improve response time for these follow-up summaries?

options.text: Enable prompt caching on the synthesis subagent to reduce the overhead of repeatedly transferring the same research findings.
Pre-generate and cache summaries at multiple granularities whenever new findings accumulate.
Spawn the synthesis subagent with reduced context and have it request specific findings from the coordinator on-demand.
Have the coordinator handle straightforward summarization requests directly using its existing context, reserving subagent spawning for complex analysis.

questions.explanation: The information is already in the context → no subagent needed. Remember: Remove the redundant step (spawning + passing 80K tokens) for a simple task.

questions.question: Reviewing a backlog of intake forms, an analyst notices that most entries name a solution rather than a need, for example "we need a dashboard.” How can Claude best help with this backlog?

options.text: Ask Claude to design the dashboard described in each entry so submitters can confirm what they wanted.
Ask Claude to group the entries by the department that submitted them and report the totals to sponsors.
Ask Claude to restate each entry as the outcome sought, then flag entries where that outcome is unclear.
Ask Claude to reject entries that name a tool and ask the submitters to resubmit them in the right form.

questions.explanation: Solution → need/outcome. Remember: Turn stated solutions into the real needs, exposing what is still unclear.

questions.question: A customer sends: "This is frustrating. I've explained my issue twice and nothing is being resolved. I want to talk to a real person NOW." The agent has not yet called any tools to investigate their account. What should the agent do?

options.text: Immediately call escalate_to_human with the conversation history.
First call get_customer and lookup_order to gather account context, then escalate to a human agent.
Acknowledge the frustration and ask one targeted question to understand the specific issue before escalating.
Briefly explain what the agent can help with and offer to resolve the issue quickly, escalating only if the customer repeats their request.

questions.explanation: The customer explicitly asks for a person → escalate immediately. Remember: Respect an explicit request; delaying makes the frustration worse.

questions.question:
A business analyst is converting a sticky-note request from a stakeholder into a structured prompt for Claude. Which is the correct order of conversion steps?
(1) Confirm the audience and the decision the response must support.
(2) Submit the structured prompt to Claude.
(3) Identify the underlying task hidden in the sticky-note language.
(4) Specify the desired length, tone, and output format.
(5) Add the supporting facts and constraints relevant to the task.
questions.explanation: Task → audience → facts → format → submit. Remember: 3, 1, 5, 4, 2.

questions.question: You are a business analyst reviewing prompt drafts written by teammates. Which two elements belong in a well-structured prompt for a business task? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: A friendly, conversational tone instruction to make responses feel more approachable
A clear statement of the task that the model must perform
A comprehensive list of company products and services to provide the model with business context
A short personal anecdote to make the prompt feel more conversational
Relevant context such as the audience and the goal of the task

questions.explanation: Task + context. Remember: The two core elements; the other options are noise.

questions.question: An HR business partner is building a long-running workspace where a team handbook, a leveling guide, and a policies-FAQ document will be referenced across many separate chats by several team members. Which Claude feature is designed for this use case?

options.text: Generate an Artifact containing the three documents, which gives the team an editable surface for the reference content that persists across chats.
Create a Project, which provides a persistent workspace with its own knowledge base and custom instructions shared across chats and members.
Attach all three documents to each chat as needed, since per-chat attachments give the chat direct access to the documents without additional setup.
Connect the team’s Google Drive folder where the three documents live, so the connector surfaces them inside each chat at the moment the chat needs them.

questions.explanation: Many chats, many people, shared documents → Project. Remember: A Project is designed for exactly this use case.

questions.question: A strategy manager is reviewing a Claude-generated recommendation to consolidate the company’s two regional warehouses into one. The recommendation cites three sources that estimate cost savings and one source confirming that consolidation is operationally feasible. Two of the source documents also contain estimates of one-time transition costs and a stakeholder concern about regional service levels, neither of which appears in the recommendation. Which concern is most warranted?

options.text: The recommendation is sound because every source it cites supports the consolidation conclusion.
The recommendation is acceptable for an initial round, but the missing material should be added in a separate appendix rather than reprompting the original output.
The recommendation should be rejected because it relies on only four sources, which is insufficient for a decision of this size.
The recommendation reflects selective use of the source documents and should be re-prompted to address the transition costs and the service-level concern before it is used.

questions.explanation: Leaving out unfavourable evidence = selective use. Remember: A source with contrary information was ignored → it must be reworked.

questions.question: You are a marketing manager deciding what to include in custom instructions for a writing-focused Project. Which two items belong in the custom instructions? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: The standard structure and the length expectations for typical deliverables
A representative sample of past writing that reflects the team’s preferred style and structure
The brand voice and the tonal expectations the writing must follow
The preferred writing style of the marketing manager who will review all final deliverables
The prompt author’s preferred response length for internal messages unrelated to external deliverables

questions.explanation: Instructions = rules; sample articles = knowledge. Remember: Rules on structure, length and tone belong in the instructions; sample articles belong in the knowledge base.

questions.question: You are a knowledge worker evaluating which Claude feature matches each proposed use case. Which two feature-to-use-case matches are appropriate? (Select two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Tool use to invoke a calculator for rephrasing a product description in simpler language.
Web search invocation to retrieve the established formula for calculating compound interest.
Long-context summarization for drafting a reply to a single short customer email.
Long-context summarization for a quarterly report distilled from many sources.
A calculator tool for complex, multi-step pricing

questions.explanation: Match the feature to the real need. Remember: Long context for many sources; a calculator for multi-step calculations.

questions.question: You are an operations lead sorting proposed Claude use cases by whether they are acceptable for your team to pursue. Which two proposed use cases are acceptable for the team to pursue with Claude? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Drafting a legal summary that an attorney will review and edit before sharing with a client
Drafting a preliminary symptom summary to support a clinician’s diagnostic review
Summarizing performance review notes across a team to support a manager’s promotion decisions
Synthesizing themes across approved customer feedback under aggregation rules
Drafting an internal training summary from approved internal documentation

questions.explanation: Low risk, approved data. Remember: Per the source key: D, E. Legal, medical and HR are sensitive areas that need their own process.

questions.question: You are an analyst working on a one-off complex problem that genuinely requires multi-step reasoning over an extended chain of thought. Which model is best suited to this work?

options.text: Opus, because it is positioned as the most capable for advanced reasoning on complex specialized tasks.
Any model, because reasoning depth does not vary across the lineup.
Haiku, because lightweight models are always preferred regardless of complexity.
A non-Anthropic model, because the Claude lineup has no option for complex reasoning.

questions.explanation: Complex, deep reasoning → Opus. Remember: Opus is the strongest tier.

questions.question: Before uploading a customer file for a Code Execution analysis, a customer-success associate at Noventra, Ltd. is reviewing the planned task. Which two practices best align with sound data handling? (Choose two.)

options.text: Confirm that the planned Code Execution task aligns with the organization’s data classification policy and escalate to the appropriate contact if the data sensitivity exceeds approved use.
Skip the upload review entirely on the basis of urgency, even though the file might contain regulated fields that organizational policy requires the user to redact before any code execution.
Review the file for sensitive, confidential, or regulated fields before upload, and remove or redact any fields that are not required for the planned Code Execution analysis.
Upload the full unredacted customer file without review, on the assumption that a sandboxed execution environment removes the need to apply the organization’s data classification policy.
Bypass the data classification policy because the task is internal, treating sandboxed processing as an exemption from the review the policy requires before sensitive data is uploaded.

questions.explanation: Sandbox ≠ exempt from data policy. Remember: Check the policy + minimise the data.

questions.question: A communications assistant receives an answer containing a clearly incorrect statement about her organisation. She corrects her own draft in a follow-up message, and also wants the problem itself recorded rather than just worked around. What should she do?

options.text: Add a line to the conversation noting that the earlier statement was wrong, so the correction sits in the chat history.
Start the same task again in a new conversation, on the basis that a clean chat is less likely to repeat the mistake.
Rephrase her original prompt in more forceful language so that the incorrect statement is less likely to recur next time.
Use the thumbs-down control on the response that contained the incorrect statement, in addition to fixing her own draft.

questions.explanation: Record the error → formal feedback. Remember: Thumbs-down sends feedback about the error; the other ways only work around it.

questions.question: A learning specialist is configuring a Project for course-design work. Their organization has an internal instructional-design standard and a preferred output structure for lesson outlines. Which custom-instruction set best supports this use case?

options.text: Name Claude’s role as a course designer, require alignment with the organization’s instructional-design standards, and specify the preferred output structure for lesson outlines.
Specify only the preferred output structure for lesson outlines, since the structure carries the standards implicitly and naming the role adds no value.
Name Claude’s role as a course designer and require alignment with the organization’s instructional-design standards; leave the output structure to Claude based on each lesson’s topic.
Name Claude’s role as a course designer; let each chat prompt specify the standards and output structure for that lesson, since lessons vary widely.

questions.explanation: Role + standards + structure. Remember: All three recurring elements, applied to every chat.

questions.question: You are designing a checklist for evaluating Claude outputs and must complete the upstream steps before scoring an output. Which two steps must be completed BEFORE scoring a Claude output against the checklist? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Define the evaluation criteria that matter for the task at hand.
Specify the threshold that distinguishes acceptable from unacceptable output.
Document the final score and the reviewer comments for the audit trail.
Forward unacceptable outputs to a senior reviewer for second-pass review.
Promote the approved output into the downstream production process.

questions.explanation: Criteria + thresholds before scoring. Remember: Without criteria and thresholds you can't score.

questions.question: A knowledge worker notices that a Claude output may have repeated a confidential financial figure from an internal source that the user was told to treat as restricted. The output has not yet been shared outside the user. Which immediate action is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue using the output for the intended internal purpose, since the figure has not left the user’s possession and no external disclosure has occurred.
Edit the output to remove the figure, save the edited version for the intended use, and document the change in a personal log without involving the governance channel.
Stop using the output and start a new chat with a more carefully scoped prompt, since the issue is resolved as long as the original output is not used.
Stop using the output, document the issue-including the prompt and the source-and report it through the documented governance or incident channel.

questions.explanation: Data incident → report through the official channel. Remember: Don't quietly handle it yourself; document it and report it.

questions.question: A procurement manager is evaluating a Claude-generated vendor proposal summary against the original RFP. The RFP lists twelve numbered requirements across pricing, security, and service levels. How should the summary be checked for completeness?

options.text: Spot-check three random requirements from the RFP against the summary, since random sampling is the standard completeness check for summaries.
Compare the section headings in the summary with the section headings in the RFP, since matching headings indicate matching content.
Map each numbered requirement in the RFP to a section of the summary and confirm that every requirement is represented.
Read the summary end to end and confirm that it forms a coherent response to the RFP, since coherent summaries typically reflect coverage of the source.

questions.explanation: Completeness = map every item. Remember: Check one-to-one against the list of requirements.

questions.question: A marketing manager is preparing a constrained brainstorming task: produce ten campaign ideas, each tied to a stated audience segment and each fitting one of three defined budget bands. Which prompting approach fits the task?

options.text: Ask Claude for ten distinct ideas, stating the audience constraints in the prompt and leaving the budget unconstrained so creativity is not limited at the ideation stage.
Ask Claude for ten distinct ideas with the audience and budget constraints stated in the prompt, and require each idea to name which audience and budget band it addresses.
Ask Claude for ten distinct ideas without budget constraints, then filter the output afterward to keep only the ideas that fit the three budget bands.
Ask Claude for thirty ideas with the audience and budget constraints stated in the prompt, then keep the strongest ten so a wider initial pool produces stronger finalists.

questions.explanation: Constraints in the prompt + labelled output. Remember: Meets the constraints directly and is easy to check.

questions.question: You are a product manager asking Claude to produce an interactive prototype of a small landing-page mockup that the team will iterate on and share. Which Claude feature is best suited to this output?

options.text: A Research run that produces a multipage external survey of competitor sites.
An Artifact, which presents standalone editable content in a dedicated side panel for iteration.
A new Project containing only the team’s prior meeting notes.
A short conversational reply embedded inline in the chat history.

questions.explanation: Interactive prototype → Artifact. Remember: An Artifact appears and is edited in its own panel.

questions.question: You are an operations lead choosing actions when a Claude conversation has degraded in quality. Which recovery action should be tried first when conversation quality degrades?

options.text: Summarize the current state and continue with a focused follow-up prompt.
Escalate to a senior architect for a manual review of the conversation history.
Replace the model with a different vendor’s model immediately.
Discard the entire conversation and rebuild the work from the original prompt.

questions.explanation: Cheapest first. Remember: A summary + a focused prompt keeps the progress.

questions.question: A knowledge worker is explaining context-window basics to a teammate. Which statement most accurately describes a context window?

options.text: A bounded amount of text the model can consider at once, including the conversation history, attached documents, and the current input.
The complete conversation history retained across sessions, which the model can reference whenever it produces a response in any chat.
The subset of the conversation that the model determines is most relevant to the current input, which can be smaller than the full conversation.
An adjustable setting that determines how much of the conversation history the model includes in each response, configurable per chat.

questions.explanation: Context window = the token limit processed at one time. Remember: Not cross-session memory, not a setting.

questions.question: A product manager is using Claude to ideate options for a new self-service portal. The team needs breadth before narrowing and will evaluate trade-offs across the options in a separate session. Which prompting strategy fits this stage?

options.text: Request multiple distinct options ordered by Claude’s assessment of feasibility, so the team can focus its trade-off discussion on the most feasible options first.
Request multiple distinct options and ask Claude to recommend the strongest one with reasoning, so the team starts the trade-off discussion from a leading candidate.
Request multiple distinct options with stated trade-offs, and avoid committing to a single recommendation in this round.
Request a single recommended option with strong reasoning, since well-reasoned single options give the team a clearer starting point than several weakly reasoned alternatives.

questions.explanation: 'breadth before narrowing' → divergent, don't settle yet. Remember: Settling early narrows the space of options.

questions.question: A prompt describes a multi-step setup process, such as configuring an environment and then running a script, but Claude sometimes performs the steps out of order. What change would make the required order unambiguous?

options.text: Provide the instructions as a numbered list of steps in the exact order they must run
Remove the step numbers and rely only on paragraph breaks to imply the correct order
Combine all of the steps into a single long sentence separated only by commas
Describe the steps in a random order and let Claude infer the correct sequence

questions.explanation: Order → a numbered list. Remember: An explicit structure removes the ambiguity.

questions.question: An operations lead creates a project on an Enterprise plan and shares it with the whole organisation. To save time she uploads a complete team folder into the project knowledge, and that folder includes a spreadsheet of individual salary bands. What is the greatest risk?

options.text: Claude will decline every request in the project while a salary document remains uploaded.
The extra documents will slow down every answer in the project until the folder has been trimmed back.
Anyone who opens the shared project can draw the salary details out through ordinary questions.
The salary spreadsheet can no longer be removed once other members have opened the project.

questions.explanation: Broad sharing + sensitive data = data exposure. Remember: The knowledge base is shared with everyone who has access to the Project.

questions.question: A business analyst is deciding whether to send one large request or break it into stages. Which two features of a request are the strongest signals that it should be decomposed? Select two.

options.text: It bundles several distinct deliverables that are meant for different audiences and uses.
Later parts are only worth producing if the earlier factual work is correct.
It concerns a subject area the analyst has not personally worked in for several years.
It runs to a long prompt because a good deal of background has been pasted in with it.
It asks for the final answer to be presented as a table rather than as flowing paragraphs.

questions.explanation: Several deliverables + sequential dependencies. Remember: Decompose so each step can be verified and each audience is served.

questions.question: A support lead finds a Claude-drafted troubleshooting article accurate but written at a reading level too advanced for the average customer. Which follow-up instruction best refines the draft without sacrificing accuracy?

options.text: Add more technical detail so customers understand the underlying cause in full
Remove the least common troubleshooting steps so the article reads a bit shorter
Convert the article into a formal specification format used by the engineering team
Rewrite the article with shorter sentences and everyday words, keeping every step accurate

questions.explanation: Lower the reading level, keep the content. Remember: Change the wording, don't cut the content.

questions.question: A retention lead asked why cancellations rose sharply in the last quarter. The answer explains at length what cancellation rates are and how they are generally measured. How should she judge this output?

options.text: As accurate but off target, because it explains the topic instead of addressing the rise she asked about.
As evidence that the question cannot be answered, since the reply avoided the specific rise she was asking about.
As adequate for now, because background on how the measure works is a reasonable place to begin the analysis.
As a sound answer that simply needs shortening, since the explanation contains more detail than she required here.

questions.explanation: Correct but doesn't answer the question = off target. Remember: Judge it by how well it meets the request, not just its accuracy.

questions.question: A marketing manager needs to draft a persuasive email campaign to launch a new product. The email should capture attention, highlight benefits, and include a call to action. Which prompting approach is best?

options.text: Prompt Claude to draft an email announcing the new product, leaving the structure and content entirely to the model’s discretion without providing any specific guidelines on audience, tone, or key product benefits to highlight.

Guide Claude to create a marketing email: first, write an attention-grabbing subject line; then, open with a hook; next, present three key benefits with persuasive language; and finally, include a clear call to action linked to the product page.

Ask Claude to produce several email drafts with distinct tones (formal, casual, urgent), then assess each draft’s persuasiveness, clarity, and brand alignment, and choose the best one for final edits, and then iterate if needed.

Instruct Claude to write a thorough product description report covering all features, specifications, technical details, and pricing info, formatted as a formal document that is suitable for internal stakeholders rather than a marketing audience.

questions.explanation: A clear structure that matches the requirements. Remember: B meets exactly the 3 requirements in the question.

questions.question: A Claude draft attributes a sentence to a named industry report as a direct quotation. What is the appropriate validation step?

options.text: Search for the sentence’s key phrase and accept it if similar wording appears anywhere.
Open the report and find that exact sentence, since a close paraphrase may not appear in it.
Ask Claude for the page number, and accept the quotation once a number has been supplied to her.
Confirm that the report exists and was published, which establishes the quotation’s origin.

questions.explanation: Direct quotation → compare word for word. Remember: A quote must match the source exactly.

questions.question: A market analyst must produce a competitor briefing drawn from many public sources, and the team will keep editing that briefing for weeks afterwards. Which two Claude features fit this job? Select two.

options.text: Turn on a mail connector first so that the competitor facts are drawn from the team inbox.
Keep the briefing inline in the chat and re-paste the newest version whenever an edit lands.
Ask for the briefing as an artifact, so the team can edit and reuse it outside the chat.
Use Research mode, so the briefing is built by multi-step searching and returns citations.
Open a separate chat for each competitor so that no single conversation ever grows long.

questions.explanation: Many sources → Research; long-term editing → Artifact. Remember: Each feature meets one of the job's needs.

questions.question: A marketer is midway through a one-off brainstorm that will not be revisited, and the conversation is approaching its limit. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Split the brainstorm across four separate chats so that no single conversation ever nears its limit.
Build a Project and move the whole brainstorm into project knowledge before writing anything more.
Let the conversation continue and condense itself, since nothing in it needs to outlive this session.
Stop the brainstorm now and restart it in a new chat so the ideas come from a completely clean window.

questions.explanation: One-off, no need to keep → let it compress automatically. Remember: Don't invest in structure for single-use content.

questions.question: A policy team keeps a handbook in a Drive folder that changes weekly, and also has one annual report that never changes. Which two set-ups fit best? Select two.

options.text: Upload the fixed annual report into Project knowledge, since its content will not change.
Paste the whole handbook into every new chat, so the newest version is always present.
Connect the Drive folder, so the weekly handbook changes are picked up from the source.
Connect the annual report and delete it from Drive, so that only one copy ever exists.
Upload a copy of the handbook just once and then rely on that copy for the rest of this year.

questions.explanation: Static → upload; changing → connector. Remember: Changing content should come from the live source; fixed content can be uploaded.

questions.question: A project shared with a Team plan workspace has just had its escalation matrix replaced with a new version. What else should the project owner do?

options.text: Ask each member to create their own copy of the project so everyone controls their own knowledge base.
Leave a note in the project title, since members are prompted to read the title before each new chat.
Tell the members who use the project what changed, so they know earlier answers may no longer hold.
Delete the project’s chat history, because past conversations would otherwise override the new material.

questions.explanation: Document changed → tell the users. Remember: Earlier answers were based on the old document; users need to know.

questions.question: A developer integrating Claude into an internal analytics agent wants to give it broad, unsupervised authority to automatically send emails and modify production database records without any human approval step. What ethical concern does this design most directly raise?

options.text: None, unless the agent is built using a third-party framework instead of Anthropic’s own official tools
None, as long as the agent uses the Claude API rather than the consumer chat product
It is acceptable because agentic use is encouraged without oversight requirements in the policy
It removes human oversight from hard-to-reverse actions, risking harm before anyone can intervene

questions.explanation: Irreversible actions + no human approval. Remember: Irreversible actions need a human in the loop.

questions.question: A Team-plan owner is uneasy about conversation content leaving the organisation when members rate Claude’s answers. What control is available to them?

options.text: Owners can have conversations redacted automatically before any rating is submitted.
Owners can set ratings to be stored only inside the organisation’s own private workspace.
Owners can switch off the chat rating feature for the whole organisation in its settings.
Owners can require that every rating is approved by a manager before it is finally sent.

questions.explanation: Admin control: turn off feedback/rating. Remember: Per the question, the owner can turn off ratings for the whole organisation.

questions.question: An operations manager has two things to add to a project: the team’s two-page approved abbreviation list, and the rule that answers must never use abbreviations outside that list. What is the best placement?

options.text: Upload both the reference list and the rule as documents in the project knowledge base, for consistency.
Put both the reference list and the rule into the project instructions so that the two are always read together.
Upload the reference to project knowledge and put the rule about unapproved abbreviations in the instructions.
Keep the reference list on the team wiki and paste the rule at the start of each chat that needs it.

questions.explanation: Reference material → knowledge; behaviour rule → instructions. Remember: Place each kind of content according to its role.

questions.question: A team lead asks whether using incognito chats on his personal plan makes it acceptable to paste regulated customer records into Claude. What is the best response?

options.text: Incognito chats are equivalent to the company’s managed workspace, so no separate approval would be required.
Incognito chats satisfy the policy, because nothing from the conversation is retained anywhere after it ends.
Incognito chats are never used to improve Claude, but the policy’s rules for regulated data still apply.
Incognito chats are acceptable for regulated data provided customer names are replaced with reference codes.

questions.explanation: Incognito ≠ exempt from policy. Remember: Data regulations still apply whatever the chat mode.

questions.question: A consultant is about to send a client a report she drafted with Claude. Her firm’s AI policy sets out several requirements for client-facing work produced with AI, and she is unsure which of them apply to a report of this kind. What should she do first?

options.text: Ask the client whether they have any objection to AI assistance having been used on the report.
Add a short line stating the report was drafted with AI assistance, and send it to the client.
Ask her engagement manager to sign the report off, so responsibility for it rests with him instead.
Establish what the policy requires for a deliverable of this kind, before the report goes out.

questions.explanation: Not sure → check the policy first. Remember: Find out which requirements apply, then act on them.
